speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 132, to incorporate the central mortgage bank.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I find that it is not necessary for m© to spend much time discussing the motion for the second reading of this bill, for the reason that on the resolution I went much more extensively into the principle than I thought I had done, and in Hansard of May 6, at page 3665, hon. members will find a reasonably complete discussion of the principle involved.
There has been some criticism of the lateness in bringing down this measure. In that connection I desire to point out that the financial resolution, after standing on the order paper for some time, was dealt with on May 6 and the bill produced immediately thereafter. I confess to the house that at
that time I had the idea that a month's adjournment of parliament was very likely, and that consequently there would be considerable time during which all interests affected across Canada would have full opportunity to study the provisions of the bill. However, we are here on the 23rd day of May and a sufficient time has, I think, elapsed to enable those who are interested in this type of legislation to gain an adequate conception of what is contemplated by the bill.
Briefly, the principle involved is the use of the national credit in adjusting the mortgage burden and in providing facilities for refinancing mortgages in the future. The bill offers to the farmer mortgage debtor, and the home mortgage debtor, below 87,000 in principal amount, a reduction in the load, which was assumed in many cases years ago undel more favourable circumstances than now prevail. The companies which become members of the bank will be obligated to write off all arrears of interest with respect to such mortgages in excess of two years' interest.
Second, the debtor will be relieved in cases where the mortgage debt exceeds eighty per cent of the value of the mortgaged property by the writing off of the excess over eighty per cent.
Third, the debtor will be relieved by the adjustment of the future rate of interest on his mortgage in those two classes I have mentioned to five per cent per annum, and an adjustment in the length of the term of the mortgage.
To the mortgage company becoming a member the plan involves that the dominion shall share over the next twenty years to the extent of one-half of the losses involved in writing off the arrears of interest and in writing down the principal, where necessary, to the eighty per cent limit. The debentures of the mortgage bank will be given to the member company, bearing interest at three per cent and running for twenty years, to the extent of one-half the losses involved in the write-down provided for by the bill. With respect to future refinancing of mortgages by member companies, to the extent that the member company takes advantage of the refinancing facilities afforded by the bill for the future, the member company must accept the conditions laid down by the mortgage bank with respect to maximum interest rates and conditions as set forth in the bill.
To the provinces this bill offers an opportunity. For a number of years past-probably for ten years-many of our provinces have felt compelled to legislate interfering with the terms of mortgage contracts. I do not believe that any provincial government has done so willingly; it has felt compelled to do

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
so by the stress of conditions which have prevailed during the past number of years. This bill offers to such provinces an opportunity to end undue interference with mortgage contracts as adjusted under the terms of this act. The bill is designed to warrant the provincial governments or provincial legislatures in exempting mortgages adjusted under this legislation from their provincial legislation which would have the effect of interfering with a contract which had been refinanced by the dominion. Obviously when the dominion credit is used in this manner it cannot be made subject to the possibility of a province impairing the dominion's security. I am certain that the provinces, after studying this legislation, will do their utmost to cooperate in giving effect to its terms, because no one is more anxious than provincial legislators, wiho by virtue of their constitutional power have been closest to matters of debt adjustment and mortgage difficulty, to get the situation regularized, adjusted and improved for the future.
Since this measure became public there has been criticism-strong criticism-from the financial press. I do not know to what extent the financial press may be said to speak for the financial organizations which are invited by this legislation to cooperate. I incline very much to the view, following more than twenty-five years' close association with various aspects of the mortgage problem, that we must move in this matter, and that the way open to us, a country governed by a federal constitution, to move must be through the channel of the voluntary action contemplated by this bill.
It will be seen at a glance that this bill exercises no compulsion upon any province. It exercises no compulsion upon any mortgage lending institution-and this, frankly, for the reason that the authority so to do does not rest with this parliament. Matters of property and civil rights, matters affecting mortgages and their terms and so on, are entirely provincial. In my judgment, therefore, we can approach this matter only through the medium of making available the national credit in terms of public need for what is generally recognized as a great national problem, not only in this country but also in the country to the south.
I do not think I can go much further in dealing with the principle of the bill. Hon. members have done me the honour, I know, of studying it, because many of them have spoken to me about it.
I do not pretend that it is an easy matter, but I believe that within the four corners of this bill we have the opportunity to remedy

very largely the confused, difficult and burdensome situation which exists across Canada with respect to mortgage credit. I am thinking to-day not merely of those who have found it impossible to meet their obligations in the terms of the obligations, and who have been compelled to rely for protection upon various provincial enactments or upon the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act; I am thinking as well of those who undertook a burden in more prosperous times and have struggled and are struggling to-day to carry that burden although it is beyond their economic strength so to do. I know from my correspondence how many hundreds of thousands of our home owners and farm owners look with hopefulness upon the measure which is now before the house for second reading, not as a means of evading their just obligations, but as a means of adjusting their honest burden to the back in a manner which will enable them the more easily to bear it.

Well do I remember the time when the people of Canada had not become educated, as they did during the war, to the buying of government bonds, when the only form of investment in the small cities of the west was by way of mortgages on farms or buildings or the homes in the small cities and towns. I believe that condition still obtains to a large extent throughout the country. This legislation offers no help either to the individual who has lent the money or to the person who has borrowed it from the individual lender in that type of case; and as a consequence it is, I think, onesided. I have here half a dozen clippings from various newspapers. I do not intend to read them all; I will merely cite the heading in the Toronto Globe and Mail:
Dominion government should hold back bill for mortgage rediscount bank until Canadians everywhere have chance to study the proposals.

Certainly I am not speaking on behalf of the financial companies. I advocate putting the legislation into such shape that it will be useful; and I submit that at this stage in the session there is no possibility of doing so. I said this privately to some of my hon. friends opposite yesterday when they were arguing, and to my mind rightly, that we should be able to finish the business of the session this week. The minister shakes his head. He did not argue that, but some of his friends did, and I agree with them. By the end of this week the session will have lasted well on towards five months, and I believe that it will be reasonable to adjourn within the next few days if we can clean up the legislation before the house- that is, if it can be dealt with in a dignified and proper manner. I submit that if this legislation goes to the banking and commerce committee, as it certainly should, it will probably take a month to deal with it there. If this legislation is to be of any real value it must include a number of these corporations. I repeat that my opinion is that in its present form it will not achieve this object.
The fact that our party favours low interest rates is proved by the existence of the Farmers' 7H92-276
Creditors Arrangement Act, which we enacted when we were in power. I entirely agree that within reason we should attempt to bring down interest rates for those who have unfortunately borrowed in the past at times when the products of, say, .the farmers were at a much higher price than they are to-day. Everybody realizes that the farmer Who borrowed money when wheat was selling at SI .50 to S2 a bushel, and now has to pay it back in bushels of wheat selling at 60 to SO cents, is certainly not in the same position to meet his obligations as he was under the price levels which prevailed at the time he borrowed the money. I believe that Mr. Bennett, as leader of the party, promised at the last election that if we were returned to power we would bring in legislation favouring the man in city or town with a mortgage on his home, showing that we also sympathize with the dwellers in the cities and towns who require relief. There is no argument, so far as I know, as to all sections of this house favouring the cutting of interest on mortgages. I say that unqualifiedly, without any hidden thought against it or anything of that sort. I am entirely for it, within reason, so long as we do not demand of loan companies that they operate at a rate upon which they cannot subsist. But I repeat that we cannot in the short time now left make this bill into legislation that will be workable. Suppose it goes to the banking and commerce committee, as it certainly should to be whipped into shape, to have the corrections made in it that legislation frequently does need. I imagine that at the very least it would take a month to hear representatives of corporations and individuals who would come forward, or who should come forward, with propositions to make this legislation useful in its application to the individual lender and the borrower from the individual lender, as well as to the financial institutions and their borrowers.
It seems to me that the clauses relating to urban and rural mortgages require greater separation and clarification than exists at present. I mention that merely as an illustration of what may be required before the banking and commerce committee in dealing with an important matter such as this. I heard some murmurs from hon. members on the other side when I said that the legislation should go before the banking and commerce committee. But if not that committee, before what committee should it go?

We say this bill provides for payment on a crop share basis. It does not say these payments shall be a distribution of assets after insolvency; on the contrary it provides for payment before insolvency, with a view to preventing such insolvency. Therefore it cannot be said to be bankruptcy legislation. In this connection I intend to refer to the matter of a reference as to whether the parliament of Canada had legislative jurisdiction to enact the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, as amended by the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1935:
In the judgment of Lord Selbourne in L'Union St. Jacques v. Belisle (1) we find, at page 38: "The fact that this particular society appears to have been in a state of embarrassment, and in such a financial condition that unless relieved by legislation, it might have been likely to come to ruin, does not prove that it was in any legal sense within the category of insolvency. And in point of fact the whole tendency of the act is to keep it out of that category and not to bring it into it. The act does not terminate the company; it does not propose a final distribution of its assets on the footing of insolvency or bankruptcy; it does not wind it up. An the contrary, it contemplates its going on, and possibly at some. future time recovering its prosperity and then these creditors, who seem on the face of the act to be somewhat summarily interfered with, are to be reinstated."
Their lordships were clearly of opinion that this was not a case for insolvency legislation, but a local and private matter within the provincial jurisdiction.
Applying this test, I would say that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is one which might be within the competence of the provincial legislature, for the same reasons, applicable in each province to each individual farmer who finds himself in difficulties, which then applied to L'Union St. Jacques, in order

Central Mortgage Bank
to enable him to carry on and, possibly at some future time, to recover his prosperity. But I cannot in view of the accepted aims and past history of the bankruptcy and insolvency legislation reach the conclusion that parliament, in passing this legislation, did not exceed the domain of bankruptcy and insolvency, to which its jurisdiction is limited. It has set up a charitable or eleemosynary institution, to be established in each separate province by proclamation; such local charities are to be established, maintained and managed under provincial legislation by virtue of 92 (7). The legislation has nothing to do directly with agriculture, with the science, the art or the process of supplying human wants by raising the products of the soil.
I submit this quotation to substantiate the argument I am making.

In addition to this clear-cut opinion I would also support my contention by the words of the right hon. Minister of Justice himself, as quoted at page 107 of L'Avenir Constitutionnel du Canada, by Mr. Ollivier:
(Translation) In most of the decisions, said Hon. Ernest Lapointe, of the privy council regarding jurisdiction which have gone against the contention of the federal parliament, it has been specially stated-and the matter is so clearly expressed in the section there can be no doubt-that those laws for peace, order and good government must be in relation to matters not coming within the classes of subjects assigned to the legislatures. Surely property and civil rights are one subject which is specifically assigned exclusively to the provinces under section 92 of the British North America Act.
And a little further on, on page 114, I find the following paragraph:
Section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, according to Lord Haldane, confers on the parliament of Canada power to deal with subjects which concern the dominion generally, provided that they are not withheld from the powers of that parliament to legislate, by any of the express heads in section 92.
(Text) It would be possible to give quite a number of quotations in support of my contention; and, as I said, this matter is so important that I believe the necessary time should be taken to put the quotations on record. In the volume to which I referred a moment ago the Minister of Justice is quoted again at page 116, as follows:
(Translation) The general power of legislation conferred upon the parliament of the dominion by section 91 of the act in supplement of the power to legislate upon the subjects expressly enumerated must be strictly confined to such matters as are unquestionably of national interest and importance, and must not trench on any of the subjects enumerated in section 92 as within the scope of provincial legislation, unless these matters have attained such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion.
These words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) which I have just quoted are also taken from L'Avenir Constitutionnel du Canada, by M. Ollivier.
(Text) Here is another striking substantiation of the point I am making; I refer to the words of Lord Haldane, also quoted in L'Avenir Constitutionnel du Canada, by Mr. Ollivier, at page 118:
(Translation) The provincial view prevailed also in the Snider case, where Lord Haldane stated: "It appears to their Lordships that it is not now open to them to treat Russell v. The Queen as having established the general principle that the mere fact that dominion legislation is for the general advantage of Canada, or is such that it will meet a mere want which is felt throughout the dominion, renders it competent if it cannot be brought within the heads enumerated specifically in section 91. Unless this is so, if the subject matter falls within any of the enumerated heads in section 92,_ such legislation belongs exclusively to provincial competency."
(Text) There is also the question of the social legislation which was referred to the supreme court, and from the texts of the various judgments rendered in that connection, I quote the following:
That the dominion may impose taxation for the purpose of creating a fund for special purposes and may apply that fund for making contributions in the public interest to individuals, corporations or public authorities could not as a general proposition be denied. Whether in such an act as the present, compulsion applied to an employed person to make a contribution to an insurance fund out of which he will receive benefit for a period proportionate to the number of his contributions is in fact taxation, it is not necessary finally to decide. It might seem difficult to discern how it differs from a form of compulsory insurance, or what the difference is between a statutory obligation to pay insurance premiums to the state, or to an insurance company. But assuming that the dominion has collected by means of taxation a fund, it by no means follows that any legislation which disposes of it is necessarily within dominion competence.
It may still be legislation affecting the classes of subjects enumerated in section 02, and, if so, would be ultra vires. In i t her words, dominion legislation, even though it deals with dominion property, may yet be so framed as to invade civil rights within the province, or encroach upon the classes of subjects which are reserved to provincial competence. It is not necessary that it should be a colourable device, or a pretence. If on a true view of the legislation it is found that in reality in pith and substance the legislation invades civil rights within the province or in respect of other classes of subjects otherwise encroaches upon the provincial field, the legislation will be invalid.

In the matter of decisions of the privy council the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said this on April 5, 1937, as reported in Hansard:
This opinion if it is valid raises grave doubts as to the validity of appropriations by this dominion parliament of current revenues for such objects as old age pensions, unemployment relief, or for giving assistance to provincial undertakings of any description. If these appropriations are illegal and beyond the competence of the dominion, grave consequence may follow, and the government would be well advised to obtain a direct decision upon this issue at a very early date.
In view of the present situation and the decisions and opinions which have been expressed from time to time by the major courts, both in this country and in Great Britain, I believe that before we attempt to pass this type of legislation we should be very careful to assure ourselves that we are not invading provincial rights or provincial jurisdiction. That is something which I am sure all hon. members will agree to safeguard. I feel that while supporting the principle of a bill of this kind, nevertheless we are bound to secure more information and to hear from all who may be interested. I feel that the question should be submitted for reference to the Supreme Court of Canada.
In connection with the Alberta legislation we find that this telegram was sent by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to Premier Aberhart on August 15, 1937. There was then in the mind of the Prime Minister a doubt as to whether or not certain legislation constituted an invasion of federal jurisdiction, and for that reason he suggested to

the premier of Alberta that such legislation should be referred to the supreme court. He did so in these terms:
Before submitting question for decision of governor in council would appreciate your letting me know whether your government would be willing to facilitate hearing of a reference to Supreme Court of Canada regarding validity of bills Nos. 5, 6 and 9 and to undertake pending determination of such reference not to take any steps towards enforcement of any of said measures.
The reference would be made under section 55 of the Supreme Court Act which provides for reference by the governor in council of important questions of law or fact touching the powers of the provincial legislatures.
Then after he had received an answer from the premier, the Prime Minister sent a telegram to the premier on August 17, 1937, indicating his decision to refer the matter to the supreme court. That telegram reads in part as follows:
2. We are advised that there is no possible doubt that the measures purporting to control banking and credit by a body or bodies appointed by the province of Alberta, and depriving individual citizens of their established right of appeal to the courts are beyond the powers of the provincial legislature and constitute an infringement upon the recognized powers of the dominion. The fact that under the constitution from which both the federal and the provincial legislatures derive their jurisdiction, the field of money and banking falls to the federal authority, has never been seriously questioned in the seventy years since confederation.
And then, paragraph 4:
4.	The issue in the present instance is that a direct attempt is being made to infringe upon a field of jurisdiction universally recognized as falling to the dominion, and to buttress this action by denying any question of the constitutionality of this section in the courts, except, I gather from your telegram, after acceptance of such illegal infringement.
5.	A reference to the Supreme Court of Canada coupled with an agreement by your government to refrain from action pending the decision, would have met the immediate case.
The point is that while the Prime Minister seemed to be in agreement with the principle of the legislation the government of Alberta was attempting to pass at that time, still, as he himself said clearly and plainly, he felt it his duty to maintain the sacred rights, as he called them, of provincial and federal jurisdiction.
There is no mention here that the Prime Minister was not in agreement or in accord with the principle of the bills he intended to refer to the supreme court. As a matter of fact we know that time and again the Prime Minister has expressed the opinion that there should be a lower rate of interest. He has also said that usury, once in control, will

wreck any nation. But when an attempt was made by a provincial legislature to deal with a problem which in their opinion affected usury in money matters, the Prime Minister did not wait to write about it but sent a telegram and carried on correspondence in that fashion. Finally, upon recommendation of the Minister of Justice to the cabinet, the legislation was disallowed.
And so we know that on many occasions in the past legislation of this kind has been questioned in the courts. For instance, we have the words of the Minister of Justice himself, which I have placed on record, to substantiate the argument I am making to-day. And for the Minister of Finance to say that this is simply a voluntary scheme does not make one iota of difference. The question is not whether the act will become operative in a province, or whether the powers given in a statute will be questioned when it is in operation. The fact that it is on the statute book, and that, provided certain conditions are fulfilled, it does give power, are to my mind clear indications that this legislation constitutes an infringement upon provincial authority.
It would be easy for us to relate what has been done in Alberta in connection with debt legislation. Those of us who come from Alberta have felt that there has been great need of a revision of interest rates and an adjustment of debt problems. But we cannot subscribe to a measure which does not take into consideration the factor of ability to pay. In a measure of this kind the debtor, in the event of his being unable to meet his obligations, immediately becomes the prey of the creditor. We know that because of the present prices of farm products, the provision for seventy cent wheat, and like matters, it is not possible for a farmer-and particularly one in the west-to meet his obligations upon a basis of this kind. Until the measure takes into account the ability of the individual to pay, then I say we should proceed with caution, because it can have no effect other than to give the mortgage company a greater hold upon the debtor.

Mr. Speaker, I have spent some time in reading and re-reading this bill and I confess that on the face of it it is quite impossible for me to ascertain the breadth of the implications of a bill such as this. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) was moving the second reading I noted that the gist of his statement appeared to be that the principle of the bill is the use of national credit in refinancing the mortgage burdens of individual mortgagors, which were undertaken in more prosperous times but the service charges of which in times of depression the mortgagors allege that they are unable to carry. That seemed to me, as I jotted it down at the time, to be the substance of his remarks. But the same considerations of policy apply to all long-term indebtedness in a country such as this, and therefore in establishing a precedent, such as this bill would establish, one must take care that we do not establish a new precedent for the dominion, whose credit is not at all times beyond question, assuming all sorts of indebtedness, provided that it is of a long-term nature, and thus open the door to a deluge of this kind of legislation. The policy in the past has been to allow individual creditors or companies to deal by compromise with individual debtors, and that policy has prevailed in this country thus far. I doubt whether it is wise now, without further consideration, to depart from that policy. Certainly this bill in its implications expresses the most extreme legislation ever brought before this parliament. It is a very, very serious measure.
The minister says that the bill makes available national credit for a great public need. That may be doubted, I think. The bill makes available public credit for private and personal needs rather than for public needs, and on that ground it should receive very serious consideration.
The proposed central mortgage bank will not be a "bank'' in the sense in which the word "bank" has been and is now used in Canadian legislation, and this new use of a word to designate a central mortgage company or corporation is confusing and, therefore, to be deplored. This so-called mortgage bank
[Mr. Cahan.J
will be another agency of the dominion government, organized chiefly for the purpose of financing the operations of loan, trust and insurance companies, in respect of loans secured by mortgages, in principal sums of any amount on farms, and in sums not exceeding $7,000 on other homestead properties.
Those companies which become members of the proposed "mortgage bank" assume certain responsibilities which may well deter responsible solvent companies from becoming members, and, on the other hand, this bill encourages companies which are on the verge of insolvency to load their liabilities upon the dominion treasury, as they will be enabled to do by this legislation.
The member company, it is true, must first cancel arrears of interest exceeding two years upon each of its existing mortgages, and then reduce the principal sum of each such mortgage to eighty per cent of the fair value of the property as hereafter appraised under the terms of the proposed act. The principal sum of each mortgage will then represent eighty per cent of the appraised value, plus arrears of interest, not exceeding two years. The principal sum of the new mortgage, as thus ascertained, will be payable with interest not exceeding five per cent per annum over a period of twenty years, or less as agreed with the government agency, by regular equal instalments of interest and principal sufficient for complete amortization of the mortgage within twenty years, or within the lesser term agreed upon with the central mortgage bank.
It is true that there are considerations given to induce these companies to become members:
1.	The central mortgage bank will assume liability to each of the companies for fifty per cent of the aggregate sums written off when the mortgages held by that company are adjusted, and issue to the company nontransferable twenty-year debentures, secured by the credit of the dominion, bearing interest at three per cent per annum, of which the principal will be paid semi-annually on an amortization plan.
2.	The central mortgage bank may buy at par or face value obligations of a member company bearing interest at 3i per cent up to the total amount of the mortgages outstanding after adjustment by that company.
3.	The central bank may subscribe for, buy and sell the preferred stock of member companies.
That, certainly, is a questionable power and should be very seldom exercised. For this

government to invest in the stock of loan and mortgage companies is a power which deserves in each case very serious consideration. The government w'ill invest $10,000,000 in the capital of the central mortgage bank, which may also issue debentures fully guaranteed by the government as to principal and interest to a total of $200,000,000. This is a prospective additional liability of $200,000,000 which may be assumed by the dominion government to pull certain of these companies out of their financial liabilities.

maintopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE BANK
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCORPORATION, PURCHASE OF SHARES, GUARANTEE OF DEBENTURES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is no doubt that legislation of this kind is necessary in Canada, and it has not become necessary only within the last two or three months; the need for it has been apparent for a good many years. This government should have been thinking about this legislation for the last four years, instead of introducing it in the dying days of the present session when there is no opportunity for proper discussion.
It is true that there has been a great deal of voluntary and a certain amount of forced adjustment of mortgages throughout Canada. It is also true that there has not been sufficient mortgage adjustment. Reasonable creditors and honest debtors have been endeavouring to get together for this purpose, and as a consequence a good deal of debt has been adjusted. If an honest debtor borrows money, with or without security, he expects to pay it back. The fact that the asset which represented his security has been wiped out does not relieve the honest debtor of his moral obligation to pay the debt if he can. If the circumstances are such that the honest debtor would be crippled by attempting to pay in full, the reasonable creditor will adjust the debt. Many of our difficulties have been brought about by unreasonable creditors and unreasonable debtors. A great deal of difficulty has been caused by unreasonable or unjudicious loans in the first place, and by a desire to exact the last pound of flesh, arising out of the necessity on the part of the creditor of maintaining his solvency. It seems to me that any legislation dealing with this matter
Central Mortgage Bank

must keep in mind the desire to maintain a high moral level. We have had legislation such as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, which was supposed to be only a temporary measure, and one has only to read Hansard to see the difficulties which have been consequent upon this legislation. We have had moratoria and other legislation of the kind on the part of the provinces subsequent to the enactment of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and we have seen advantage taken of this legislation both by creditors and by debtors. If a creditor is without reasonable assurance that his principal will be repaid, irrespective of legislation he is not going to lend his money. This is the case to-day in some parts of Canada. If we look back to some of the causes of the present position of the private debt burden, we find mistakes that were made both by lenders and by borrowers. Many lenders and borrowers did not properly anticipate the future. The lender was willing to lend at high rates of interest on inflated values, and the borrower was anxious to borrow under those conditions in the prospect that he would be able to make sufficient profits to take care of the price he had to pay for the money. They were botl willing, but high taxes and low income returns increased the burden and decreased the ability to pay, with disastrous results both to the borrower and to the lender. Under these circumstances it is necessary and proper that the plight of both borrower and lender should be taken into consideration and government aid of some kind given. But we must remember that if government aid is to be given, the people of Canada must pay for it. Someone has to pay. On the other hand if this accumulated burden can be lightened there will be in consequence a general revival of business which will benefit all the people, and so the government is justified in the contribution thus made.
I am in favour of the general principle of the bill, but not of the attempt under the bill to control future interest rates. Rigid control of future interest rates would mean a drying up of the wells of money for the more speculative classes of loans.
Then there is complaint that it is difficult to get mortgage money except in large centres. This bill will aggravate that situation. The machinery for the adjustment of interest rates is with us in Canada to-day through the Bank of Canada, through its control of the quantity of money. It can and will control this, therefore it is bound to control interest rates- not by establishing a fixed rate, but by recog-

nizing a general rate which from time to time is considered good for the people of Canada.
This bill to my mind does not meet the needs of the present time. It is likely to become another Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, with all the consequences which followed that measure. It should be sent to the banking and commerce committee to be properly discussed. The formation and setting up of a central mortgage bank will have just as far-reaching consequences as the formation of the Bank of Canada had, and calls for just as careful consideration by all parties interested as was given to the formation of the Bank of Canada. There is no doubt about the present need for this organization; as I said before, it has been obvious at least since 1935.
The bill, as has been said before, is applicable only to companies which decide to become members of the bank. I think there will be very few that will become members. Moreover, only those mortgagors whose mortgages are held by member companies will receive the advantages the measure seeks to provide.
What are the advantages to the companies on an injudicious loan? Suppose a mortgage claim, including interest, is $4,000, and the present value of the property is S3,000. The write-down would be to 80 per cent of the present value, or 82,400. The write-off would therefore be SI ,600, and the company would receive half of that amount, or $800, in government bonds. The result would be that on a loan on which it would have lost $1,000, the company now has a mortgage of $2,400 and $800 in government bonds, or a gain of $200.
What about the mortgagor? He benefits to the extent of 81,600. But how about the unfortunate mortgagor whose mortgage is held by a non-member company? He is at a disadvantage. There is direct discrimination under this bill to the extent of SI,600 as between those two mortgagors. It is true that all the mortgagors to the member company will benefit by the reduction in the interest rate and the write-down under this legislation. But what about the other mortgagors whose mortgages are held by non-member companies?
Again, what is the advantage to the company? I have some figures, slightly altered in proportion, which are estimated to be fairly accurate, with regard to one life insurance company. If this company becomes a member of the bank there will be a writeoff, in round figures, of 82.000,000, of which the company would get half in government

Central Mortgage Bank
bonds, or $1,000,000. They would bind themselves to an interest rate of five per cent in future. They would lose in interest by the write-down an annual amount of $200,000. They would not become a member of the bank. As a matter of fact the people who would lose would be the policyholders of this company, because this would mean a very large reduction in its profits. This company has already adjusted its mortgages two or three times with respect to both interest and write-down. Even if the company were offered the bait of getting back the write-off that has already taken place, to which I should think they should be entitled, there would not be sufficient inducement to the company to make it desire to become a member of the central mortgage bank.
There is no desire on the part of the majority of mortgagors to ask for the forgiveness of their debt. Why then should the bill be so comprehensive as to force this adjustment at the expense of the policyholders of Canada? To substantiate what I said a few moments ago, I should like to point out that the premium rates on life insurance policies [DOT] are based on the cost of doing business, the life expectancy of the policyholders and the interest rate that can be earned on money invested. The interest rate that most companies consider necessary in order to carry on is 3i per cent. The cost of doing mortgage business runs between one and one and a half per cent, not taking into account any losses which may be incurred. On properties adjusted on the monthly amortization plan over a twenty year period there will be an added cost of at least one-quarter of one per cent, though it is possible that the losses under the monthly payment plan may be less than under the present system. It simply means that this company could not afford to become a member; or, if it did, it would no longer consider it worth while to invest money in mortgages but would invest in bonds and other securities of the kind.
Now I should like to give a few figures with regard to life insurance in Canada. Under the industrial plan we had in this country at the end of 1937 some 4,012,358 policies amounting to $895,299,984, or an average of $233 per policyholder. On the ordinary plans there were 2,470,064 policies in force amounting to $5,178,127,114, or an average of $2,096 per policy. These are the people who are going to bear the burden of this mortgage readjustment. The companies have some $417,238,000 invested in mortgages and sales agreements in Canada, and the scaling down of the interest rate which would take place under this
scheme if these companies became members would amount to $4,172,238. That is the annual interest loss they would suffer by becoming members. So that they will not become members of the bank if the bill remains in its present form.
Then the act provides that if a province passes legislation satisfactory to the central mortgage bank with respect to the mortgages adjusted, the member company shall be obliged so to adjust mortgages in that province. If in any year subsequent to a company becoming a member restrictive legislation should be passed, that company would have no protection or guarantee with respect to such mortgages as had already been adjusted. Again the companies could not possibly enter into a scheme of this kind under those conditions, because in the meantime they might have made further loans on the new basis.
Then the central mortgage bank must make the appraisals, of which there will be thousands. Where are we to get all the appraisers who will be needed? I do not think we have enough of them in Canada at present to take care of the situation. There will also be appeals to be heard; we will have thousands of appeal boards all over the country. One company I have in mind might require anywhere from one thousand to fifteen hundred men on these boards in one province, and they must pay these men. Of course the government pays all the other members of the appeal boards, but believe me we are going to have plenty of appeals. In addition there is no doubt that there will be general dissatisfaction with the appraisals that are made, and how long will it be before the mortgagors will demand the right to appeal also? At present, with the bill as it stands, only the companies have the right to appeal, but before long the mortgagors will insist on that right also. The tendency of appraisals is bound to be downward, with consequent depreciation of property values all over the country. I do not see any other possible result. A man who has his house appraised will try to have the appraisal low, and immediately the property next door will take on the same value. Low values are to the advantage of the debtor.
To sum up, in my opinion the bill does not meet the need at the present time. It discriminates against individual classes of mortgagors, and will force adjustments in many cases where they are not necessary. The other day I met a friend of mine on the street who said, "Isn't it kind of the government to try to give me some money?" He went on to
Central Mortgage Bank

say, "The company have adjusted my mortgage, and I am quite satisfied with the rate of interest. I have a S6,000 mortgage, though the value of my property has depreciated to $5,000. As a matter of fact I am quite willing and able to pay the debt and the interest as it has been adjusted, but what would you do if you were me? I understand that my mortgage can be adjusted to eighty per cent of the present value, which would be $4,000; in other words I can get a present of $2,000 from the company and the government if I decide to take it." That is the situation under this scheme. The only people who are going to be stuck, as this gentleman said, are the policyholders of the company.
As I say, this bill does not meet the present needs. I think it is simply designed to fool the public. I protest against its being passed in its present form. I do not think this is anything more or less than a plain, ordinary vote-catching measure, put out on the dying days of a session. The consequences being so far-reaching, the bill should be most carefully and thoroughly discussed. After all, those who are managing the affairs of life insurance companies have in their trust enormous funds of policyholders-and when we speak of the policyholders we mean, of course, the public. Those policyholders have the right to be heard through the managers of the insurance companies.
I cannot express adequately my views respecting the move made by the government in bringing in a bill of this kind without having first consulted representatives of policyholders. There is no doubt that there is need of some readjustment. I realize that there are many people even in my own constituency who need and are deserving of relief of some kind. I am in favour of giving it to them, but this bill will not help them; on the contrary it will only get us into a sad mess of grief. It is ill-advised, and, as I have pointed out before, no life insurance company can afford to enter into the proposed agreement; so that under this measure it will be impossible to make any adjustment in respect of mortgages totalling a value of $417,000,000.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to the amendment offered by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) to the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) to the proposal of the government to raise a loan of 8750,000,000.
Once more we are carrying on a discussion of monetary matters. To people who see things as I and those who agree with me see them, there is no possible solution of the problems that confront us as a nation, or of those that confront the world, until we acquire a more realistic view of the whole question of money and financial administration.
There are several questions at issue in this dominion which have been at issue since I first came to Ottawa, and doubtless before I came here. These questions all centre around the main question:	Can a state or
a government safely create, issue and use debt-free money?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What does that mean?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I should be much
better pleased to define it later, but since the hon. member has raised the question I will give an illustration. At page 22 of the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, published in 1933, the hon. member will find a statement to the effect that between 1915 and 1917 the Canadian government printed 826,000,000 of bills and used them for general purposes. Behind 810,000,000 of those bills there was nothing but the credit of the country. Behind the other 816,000,000 there was nothing but worthless railway securities, securities of no value whatsoever except as the dominion government stood behind them. I contend that that 826,000,000 was debt-free money and interest-free money. That will serve as a concrete instance for the hon. member to keep in his mind all through this discussion.
Just as soon as that 826,000,000 can be explained away, the opponents of the policy
440P
Loan of $,750,000,000

which I advocate will be at least that far along the way to establishing their case. But until they can show that the issue of that 826,000,000 was pernicious and not in the interests of the country, the facts of the case stand against them. Until they can explain why that 826,000,000 might not just as well have been S36,000,000 or S56,000,000 or $106,000,000, I maintain that they are completely impotent to challenge successfully the principles which we as a group advocate. So much having been said, I proceed.
There are three main questions concerning which the house is exercising itself: (1) Will such money as the $26,000,000 cause inflation? (2) Will such money have an adverse effect on the exchanges to the detriment of Canada's trade? (3) If the government commences to issue and to use such money, can the government control the issue so that it will not go to extremes?
Let me deal with the third question first. I refer again to the $26,000,000. The Dominion of Canada undoubtedly had the absolute power to issue five times $26,000,000, but it did not do so. The Dominion of Canada at that time was reputedly a democracy. If a democracy could control itself during the stress of war, it seems reasonable that it could control itself when there is no such stress.
Before proceeding to discuss the question in detail I should attend to several points raised in the debate. Some of them were raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, some by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), and some by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). First let me say that we have no particular objection to the subamendment of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Our group is prepared to support his amendment. An issue of $100,000,000 is not sufficient by any manner of means. Nor was he quite prepared to say that he was willing to issue it debt free, as the $26,000,000 was issued when Canada was at war. But he did seem to be in favour of issuing it interest free, thereby laying down a principle which is more generous and more realistic than the principles which at the present time govern the financial operations of this dominion. Consequently we are disposed to support the subamendment, feeling that by so doing we are helping to establish the principle of debt-free money.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in common with a great number of other hon. members, in spite of everything which can be said to the contrary, in spite of pages by the score in Hansard, persists in maintaining
[Mr. Blackmore.l
that the Social Credit party favour issuing money without reepect to goods and services. That is a fallacy and an absolute misconception; for, from the time we came here until the present, we have never advocated the issuing of money without reference to goods and services. When we first came here we maintained that there was a shortage of purchasing power in the hands of the people. What does that mean? It means that there is too little purchasing power in the hands of the people to enable them to buy the goods and services which are available to be bought -which by implication clearly argues or contends that there is a surplus of goods and services. By issuing new money, all you are doing is matching the goods and services which are now surplus and a drug on the market with corresponding financial tickets to enable the people to obtain those tickets to buy the goods and services which are now surplus and not saleable. I assume I shall have to lay this down a hundred times more before I can get it into the minds of men like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that the purpose of social credit is to create tickets or financial counters to represent goods and services which are available in the land to-day and which are neither purchasable nor marketable because there is a lack of purchasing power in the hands of the people.
May I read a short quotation from a speech of the hon. member to show him why I have interpreted his remarks as I have done. He said, as reported at page 4065 of Hansard:
When I say that, I realize that money has some basis in fact, some basis in real goods and services. I think the mistake our friends often make when discussing monetary reform is, as I have said before, that they tend to mistake the shadow for the substance.

speechtext:
There is nothing
particularly wrong except that in the light of the. facts it is pure nonsense and absolutely false. In one of the first speeches I delivered in this house I pointed to the fact that in the United States in a given year, which at that time I did not know to be 1918, there were consumable goods to the value of 60 billions of dollars, but there were only 40 billions of available purchasing power to buy the goods. The result was that there were 20 billion dollars' worth of goods which the people of the United States were unable to get purchasing power to buy. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) will remember this quite distinctly, because he took the illustration which I gave and, leaving out entirely the authorities I quoted, so as to leave me entirely to the winds of criticism,

Loan oj $750,000,000
wrote the whole matter up for the delectation of people all over Canada. I remember quite distinctly, however, that the incident establishes conclusively the stand we took, that we have in mind only the issuing of purchasing power when there are goods and services which are surplus.
There is another statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar with which I shall deal, I refer to page 4066 of Hansard, and will read certain words which he used:
"Free of debt" is really a misnomer. The moment a dollar is issued by the government it is a demand for a dollar's worth of someone's goods or services. Somewhere in our economy someone will have to pay a dollar's worth of commodities or goods to me, the demand for which I hold at the moment, and which is their debt to me temporarily.
Now the hon. member is at perfect liberty to interpret "debt free" in that way if he desires. But if I have a cow, for example, and a man comes to me and offers me S75 for that cow, one of the last things I ever think of is that that S75 is a demand for the cow, that is, that I owe the man who has the $75 my cow. I say he is buying my cow and I am very glad to get the $75.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: You are going to put water in the milk, though.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I hope that Hansard got that remark and the hon. member who made it. That is all I wish for the hon. member who makes such a nonsensical remark as that.
If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is going to look upon the $26,000,000 as debt, I do not mind taking his definition, but I do not look upon this money as debt to anybody, unless it should be to the government. At the present time every dollar of debt which Canadians issue and use is a debt, in a very real sense, to a bank or a financial institution. The social crediters contend that if you are going to call the money debt, it must be to the government and not to a bank. An illustration of this in monetary history is the Bradburys of England. The British government fought the war and won it with a unique type of paper currency which was issued by the government debt free, was sold at its face value to anyone who chose to buy it, and was backed by nothing except what was known as the treasury notes redemption fund, of which we shall talk later, probably, if we have the occasion or the opportunity. I have heard once or twice hon. members make the statement here that never has there been a government issue of money which did not result in inflation. Now we can challenge any hon. member to show that the Bradburys caused inflation.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Who said-in the house -that there has never been an issue which did not cause inflation?

speechtext: I have not under my hand the reference to Hansard. I have the particular hon. members in mind, but I would not name them without verifying it.

speechtext: Then do not say it; that is all.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: From which I gather that there is no one here who is prepared to say that state-created paper money has not sometimes succeeded.

speechtext: In doing what?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
In financing the affairs of the country. Once we grant that the Bradburys of England were a state-created paper money, and were sound, and did not cause inflation, and did not disturb the exchanges, we have gone a tremendous distance towards acknowledging the fundamental soundness of the social credit contention.
It is said that when a dollar is issued by a government somebody has to pay for the dollar-has to "pay the goods." Is that not equally true if the Bank of Canada issues a dollar? If, for instance, the Bank of Canada issues $100 and with that $100 buys gold, the man who takes the $100 for the gold has a demand on anybody's goods. He can go to the farmer next door and buy hay with the money. But no one looks upon that $100 as making the farmer owe the hay. Usually the farmer is very glad to get a market and happy to take the money; he never looks upon the money as being a debt which he has to pay. The thinking of some hon. members has become, to say the least, somewhat warped.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The contention is
made, and has been made if I remember correctly by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) that somebody has to pay one dollar's worth of goods or services for that dollar. The same will be true of each dollar of the $750,000,000 which the minister proposes to borrow. At the same time the people of Canada must not only supply goods and services for each of those dollars, but they must be taxed to pay interest on it. They then must be taxed to pay the dollar back, so that instead of owing one debt they will owe three.
Loan of $750,000,000

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman fails to distinguish between demand obligation and deferred obligation.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The minister worries about the demand obligation. When the Bank of Canada issues $100 with which to buy gold or securities, no one worries about that so far as demand for his goods is concerned. I do not have to take any man's dollar for my goods and services unless I choose to do so. The important fact is that the money is there so that I can take it in case I want it, but there is no law compelling me to take it. So much having been said in this regard, we will go on. I hope we hear no more of this argument that somebody has to pay goods for dollars created.
In a passage between the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar I gathered that the minister was much concerned about the effect on the tariff which would result from the issuing of new money, and the effect it would have on exchanges. It is altogether impossible for anyone to see, if he stops to think, how there could be any greater influence on the tariff as a result of the creation of new money than there would be in consequence of the circulation of borrowed money. Surely if the money is to be spent it will have the same effect on prices when it is borrowed as it would have if it were created; and if you do not increase the prices of goods you will not affect either the exchanges or the tariff. The controlling factor is the prices of goods in the country. I repeat, you cannot affect either the tariff or the exchanges unless you affect the price level within the country. If money can be created and issued in the country without raising prices, it will have no more adverse effect on ' tariff and exchange than if it were borrowed and spent in the country. This is a vital consideration in the whole study of monetary theory.
It is taken for granted by a good many people that the moment a government issues new money it depreciates the currency. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) implied something of the sort when he said that we would be watering the milk. When the hon. member for Brant knows a little more about money he will not say that. When the Canadian government created the $26,000,000 and put it into circulation in Canada it did not water the money Canada had in circulation any more than it would have done if it had borrowed the money from the banks and spent it. That is another misconception that exists in the minds of men; and in the very minds that cherish that misconception in its 
grossest form there is the greatest indisposition to pay any attention to reason on questions of money.
There will never be depreciation of money in the country provided there is an increase in goods and services to match the new money. That is a fundamental truth. As a matter of fact, if you increase goods in the country without increasing the money you cause prices to fall. The hon. member for Brant will readily understand that. If you doubled the potato crop in Canada you would cut down the price; if you doubled the sugar crop, if you doubled the production of wheat or of coal or of any other commodity, you would reduce the price. If you could double the production of every commodity you would cut the price in half, or very considerably.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
And if you doubled the money it would have the same effect. It works both
ways.

speechtext: I will give a quotation for my hon. friend by and by. The time will come when we shall all be converted to the view I am now stating because it is the only common sense attitude to take. speechtext: It did work in an astonishing way. When the time comes I will answer my hon. friend and he will not need a second answer.

speechtext: You take four years to answer.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
We were dealing with an increase in commodities. When you double the production of wheat and of every other commodity in the country, unless you double the amount of money you will have a fall in prices; but if you double the amount of money or greatly increase it to match the

Loan of $750,000,000
increase in the goods produced, you will not have a fall in prices, nor will you have any depreciation in money. This is the fact which hon. members lose sight of. We have entered an age of plenty in which we can readily increase goods far beyond any point to which we could ever increase them in times past, and therefore we must be able readily to increase the money counters to match the goods or we shall have a fall in prices, called depression.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Then you would increase production as the money increased.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes. That would happen automatically. It is well known that when you increase the money in circulation there follows an increase in the quantity of goods produced.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question after listening to his explanation of his monetary theory. When the government prints enough of these money tickets he speaks of, for the purchase of surplus goods and services, will not production pile up a further surplus of goods and services, and therefore will it not be necessary at once to print more money tickets? If this is done, will not the circle go on expanding into an unlimited, uncontrolled inflation?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is an excellent question. The hon. member has moved in the direction of correct reasoning. Just as soon as the government increases the money tickets there will be at once greater production. As soon as that greater production of goods takes place there are plenty of goods and services to absorb all the money without any rise in prices. That is one of the very factors that would prevent inflation, provided the right people got the tickets. I will come to that later. Social credit has proposed that the money shall be distributed to the consumers in the form of dividends or price adjustments. Can you imagine a better place in which to put the money than right there? The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar the other day made a strong appeal for the spending of the money in public works in order that it might find its way to the consumers.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: And the country would have something in return.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Perfectly true. If the money goes out into the hands of consumers and they buy and consume and thereby cause the producer to produce more, has not the country something to show for it? If the country has more butter, cheese, coal and all that sort of thing, surely that is better.
Now, to show that there are a good many people who are thinking just along the lines that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) suggested by his question let me read a statement from Senator Owen, who was head of the finance committee of the United States senate. This statement was made on June 9, 1937 in the United States senate committee on farm commodity prices.
I read from page 141 of the report of that committee:
It is a matter of supreme importance to keep in mind and at all times to remember, that when you double production it has a tendency to decrease the market price of commodities and thereby to offset the rise in the price of commodities which would take place as a result of expanding the money supply. So long as the expansion of the money supply results in the expansion of employment and increased production of commodities, the one offsets the other. The commodity index is diminished by the increase of commodities unless the money supply increases at the same time.
Just as I pointed out to the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood).
Increasing the money supply will absorb the unemployed until maximum production is achieved. Maximum production and the absorption into private industry should be our objective.
I remember there was one point raised by the hon. member for Davenport with which I did not deal. He said you would not be able to go on because as you issued money you would increase production and would have to go on until you had inflation. Let us bear in mind that you have inflation only when you have more money in circulation than the goods and services to be purchased. The hon. member's idea was a progressive increase of goods and services beyond the amount of money you have, which indicates a tendency to progressively falling prices instead of rising prices in a land of abundance such as Canada. One of the fundamental principles of the system which we advocate lies right there. Let us remember that we are in a land of abundance, a land of great resources, and in an age when we can produce goods more abundantly and more quickly than ever before in the world's history. We are in a country bountifully provided with machinery of many different kinds, many industries running only part time. The result is that conditions here are ideal for the introduction of the principles of monetary reform. So that then there will be no inflation so long as there are unemployed men and machinery and resources.
I am going to quote two or three men whose names and records entitle them to some respect. First I quote Paul H. Douglas in his book,
Loan of 50,000,000

Control of Depressions. He is professor of economics at Chicago university. On page 148 he uses these words:
Finally if we turn to actual experience we find it simply is not true that the use of paper money invariably leads to runaway inflation.
Hon. members may disregard my words, but he is a reckless man who disregards the words of a man like that.

speechtext: Wait until he is done. I quote from the same author again. Incidentally I am just going to accept the challenge of the hon. member. If he will let me call for a book I will read to him something regarding this same man which will startle him.

speechtext: Never mind; dispense.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I read now from page 126:
It is indeed on just such points as these that many so-called orthodox critics of a public works program miss the point.
We are arguing directly along the line of the resolution of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
They tend to assume that all the workers and all of the productive plants are already fully employed and that the creation of additional monetary purchasing power merely increases the money counters for a constant supply of goods, and hence results in a proportionate increase in the price level which cuts down the effective purchasing power of others in the same degree as it builds up the buying power of those on public works.
The real truth is very different. There is much unemployment and a tremendous amount of unutilized capital. The creation of this additional monetary purchasing power enables the two to be brought together, and more goods to be produced. The volume of production increases at the same time as (and indeed because of) the increase in this purchasing power-
The hon. member for Davenport will be pleased to notice this.
-and should increase by very much more than the initial expenditure by the government. Prices, therefore, need not increase by anywhere near the ratio of the proportion of increase to the monetary supply.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: If the wheat crop of western Canada were doubled, what would the hon. member do with it?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Now that brings in the question of surpluses which the country is unable to use. That is another matter which has to be dealt with in a different way.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Yes, I know the loud foolish "ha-ha's". But the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) will readily remember that in Canada we are not producing anywhere near the amount of honey that we could produce and that the people of Canada could use; we are not using anything like the amount of milk that the people of Canada could use, and there are many other commodities of which enough is not produced, or of which we are not enabling our people to consume enough. It is on that kind of commodity that the effort would have to be concentrated, as I pointed out in the wheat debate, drawing production away from wheat and diverting it to the production of goods which we need and can consume within our own country.
If the hon. member will let me proceed I will deal with his question again at a later time. But the problem of surplus production of a wide variety of products in Canada must be met and solved, and I contend that the hon. member or his party have no solution which is as good as the one I have offered by any means. They are faced with an absolute blank in the matter of dealing with this surplus production. Unless he thinks more than he has said, which probably is the case, his policies would lead to a decrease of the amount of wheat produced, with the result that a large number of farmers who now are producing wheat on the plains of western Canada would be thrown out of employment and on relief.
Since the hon. member for Melfort raised the question whether this man Paul H. Douglas advocates a distribution of money, let me tell him that on page 279 of this book, at the bottom of the page, he can read under division 10 and 11 the following:
10.	The establishment of a system of unemployment insurance so managed that there would be an attendant transfer of purchasing power from periods of prosperity to those of depression.
11.	The use of a social dividend to consumers or an increased expenditure upon cultural services, if the amounts distributed to the purchasers of mass production goods are not sufficient to consume at a profit to industry and under competitive prices the mass production goods and services which are turned out by industry.
The fine progressive thinkers in every part of the world are seeing the necessity of the principles which we advocate.
Let me now turn to the words of another important man whom I am sure no hon. member will recklessly disregard; I refer to Right Hon. Reginald McKenna. In an address delivered at the annual meeting of the bank

Loan oj $750,000,000
on January 29, 1936, as printed in the Monetary Review of January-February 1936, he is reported as saying:
We learnt that a shortage of money may be just as vicious in its effects as an excess though deflation has still a touch of virtue about it in the minds of many people. Nevertheless it is becoming more and more widely recognized that greater productivity calls for an increased supply of money for otherwise prices will fall, business will stagnate and the growing productive capacity will be unused.
How admirably he pictures the unfortunate position in which we in Canada find ourselves to-day. Later he says:
For money to be truly sound there must be enough of it to finance ordinarily growing volume of trade, yet not so much as to give rise to an inflationary movement of prices.
Perfectly true; I do not contend anything else. All I maintain is that under the present system, by which Canada- issues money to consumers and producers only through bank loans, it is impossible for people to borrow enough from the banks to enable them to buy the goods which are there to be bought. Consequently there must be brought into play money from another source, which does not come out of a bank as debt.
The misuse of gold has driven us to abandon fixity of the external value of our currency for a more important benefit of stable internal value. Whereas since 1931, the pound sterling has depreciated by 40 per cent; in terms of gold currencies its purchasing power in the hands of the consumer has been practically unchanged.
Here is another man who has his eyes on realities. That is all we are asking, that the members of this house keep their eyes on the realities of to-day instead of the realities of seventy-five years ago. Now I am going to read another quotation from Senator Owen.
