speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as I have not yet spoken on this amendment, I should like to make some observations on it; and inasmuch as I was unable to finish my speech on the previous amendment I shall continue it now.
A good deal was made of the fact that the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) proposed that $600,000,000 in new money be issued to pay debts. There seems to be an idea that if the government of Canada should issue $100,000,000 of bills to pay off debts, immediately there would be some serious result. I ask how there could be any such result. Let us suppose we took $50,000,000 of the $100,000,000 with which to buy back bonds. Then the money issued to buy back those bonds would go into the banks, and would become additional reserves of the banks, upon which those institutions might create a quantity of credit. The fear that is expressed is that the creation of the credit by the banks at the rate of ten to one would cause inflation. Let hon. members of the house bear in mind that a bank cannot create credit at the rate of ten to one unless it can find a borrower. To-day the banks cannot find enough borrowers to use the money they already have in their possession. How in the world would an increase in the reserves of the banks to the extent of $50,000,000
Loan of $750,000,000

enable the banks to create other loans until available borrowers presented themselves? All arguments concerning inflation on that score are idle because they are not realistic, they do not face the facts of the situation, which is that to-day the banks cannot find enough borrowers.
It is contended that if the government once starts there will be a great tendency to issue more money. That will not be so. The only reason popular pressure has been brought to bear on the government to issue more money is that the people have been ignorant. Once the people as a whole realize that there is only so much money to be issued, that the amount that can be issued depends upon the surplus goods and services which are in the country but which are not being sold, immediately the pressure will cease; for no intelligent populace is going to ask its government to do a foolish thing. People point to the experience in connection with the assignats. Before we get through to-day I intend to point out that even the people who were in charge of the assignats, the very people who were issuing them, the most intelligent people of the period, had not the slightest idea what gave the assignats value. They thought money was given value by land behind it, while as a matter of fact money is given value only by the use a country has for that money; and that use depends upon the power of the people to produce and consume goods and services. Only in the last few years have our most learned men come to realize that. Just as soon as this parliament understood that that was the secret which determined how much money it could issue, you would not get a man in this parliament to vote for the issue of a dollar beyond the safe limit. And the mere fact that to-day they are' so tenaciously resisting the issue of money is clear evidence that the members of this parliament realize their responsibility and are prepared to accept it according to their understanding.
The very first thing a social credit administration would do would be to have a national account drawn up showing in the minutest detail the goods and services on hand which were not being bought, so that everyone would know how much money could be issued. The limit would be set by the limit of the goods and services available.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: How would you do that?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
By bookkeeping, just as the bureau of statistics can tell us so many facts to-day. Even the bank reports show us at what percentage of productive capacity

the various industries of this country are working. How can they tell that? If they can give that information surely they can ascertain the amount of surplus goods those various industries have in their storerooms, and the amount the various wholesalers have on their shelves. The very first thing that would be done by a social credit administration would be the compiling of a national credit account, showing exactly where the nation stood physically-the number of surplus shoes, the amount of surplus coal, the surplus of cream, butter, and all that kind of thing.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: How can you measure the productive capacity of Alberta, for example, in regard to coal?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Inasmuch as it happens that I have a good deal of other material which I believe is of greater importance than an answer to the hon. member's question, I would ask permission to disregard his question until the end of my speech. I would say however that that is an easy matter to-day, when there are people who are skilled in figures to attend to it.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: How do you measure the surplus of agricultural products?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
How do you measure the surplus of wheat which remains unsold? We glibly talk about this matter, for every informed person in the country knows the amount of the wheat surplus held as a holdover or carry-over. Only the other day we were talking about a surplus of butter in Canada, and about the issuing of vouchers to use a quantity of that butter to reduce the surplus. To raise a question like that is to reveal puerility.
Let us put it this way: Let us suppose that $750,000,000 of money which is now idle in bank vaults, and not being used, is brought out as new money-and it would be new money, would it not? If that were done, I wonder if anybody would be afraid of inflation? We will suppose we were to distribute the $750,000,000 on a per capita basis throughout the provinces, giving each province its fair share. In that event is there any person in the house or in Canada who would be afraid that there would be inflation? On the contrary, all would rejoice. The great difficulty is that we have not the money throughout the country. There is a decrease of money in the hands of agriculturists.
One matter was raised by the Minister of Finance with which I shall have to deal. He indicated that the monetary matters of this dominion had to be governed by the will of

Loan of $750,000,000
other nations. Mr. Speaker, once we grant that principle we are granting that this parliament has no power to govern Canada.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
If this country cannot manage its own financial affairs without deferring to other countries, then I say Canada has lost the power of self-government. I do not think the minister would care to commit himself to any such proposition.
I shall refer again to the words of Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, which I read previously, to the effect that money in England had fallen in terms of gold forty per cent, but that it had retained its internal purchasing power. The thing which affects Canada is the internal purchasing power of the dollar, just as in England the most vital thing was the internal purchasing power of the pound.
The leader of the opposition had a good deal to say about assignats. I think I must spend a little time on a discussion of assignats. I am sorry I do not see the hon. member in his seat, but I presume he has gone out to perform some of his many duties. What I have before me would be of great value to him. I judged from the reaction across the floor of the house, when the hon. member was mentioning assignats, that the incident connected with assignats is being used by a certain element of the Liberal party to beat down the monetary reformers. They will be glad to learn some of the facts which I shall point out. First of all I shall quote from the very book from which the leader of the opposition quoted. I happen to have spent about six weeks in rather intimate contact with the same author.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: And wasted a lot of time.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
That remains to be proved. I believe the reverse will be proved in a very few minutes. I turn first to page 1 of the book. It is there stated that under conditions which existed before they commenced to issue assignats:
There was a general want of confidence in business circles; capital had shown its proverbial timidity by retiring out of sight as far as possible; throughout the land was stagnation.
It is important, sir, to point out that those conditions existed before the assignats were issued, because by and by, after the assignats collapsed, for a variety of reasons, the fact that conditions like that returned to the country was used as an argument against assignats.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What is the hon. member's authority? Put it on the record.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: It is the book quoted by the leader of the opposition, entitled Fiat Money Inflation in France, written by Andrew Dickson White.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: How do we know that those are facts?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Well, it is the material used by the leader of the opposition. I have come in contact with this book in every citadel of high finance I have ever entered in Canada, and it has been cited as the absolute evidence that all my theories were an indication of foolhardiness. So if it is accepted by those people I suppose it would be safe enough to accept it to prove what I am saying. When there happens to be some evidence on our side, then certainly I suggest we ought to be permitted to take advantage of it.
I draw attention particularly to three facts herein set out. Capital had retired out of sight, as far as possible. This is the thing which they say will happen when we have inflation. Then it is said that there was a general want of confidence in business circles. That is the sort of thing that is supposed to happen when we have inflation. And then it is stated that throughout the land there was stagnation.
I shall read another quotation. Implications and innuendoes have been thrown out in the house on many occasions to the effect that social crediters are an ignorant lot, and do not know much about the facts. I shall read from a book entitled The Encyclopaedia of Social Sciences, volume 2, page 279-this book is available in the parliamentary library. An article written by G. Salvemini, bearing upon assignats, has this to say:
In the early stages of the revolution the national assembly was confronted with a large public debt, inherited from the aneien regime, and a growing deficit in the current budget. As a matter of principle it would not repudiate the former, and for reasons of political expediency it could not raise taxes. It appealed to the nation for a contribution patriotique and pending the sale of crown and church lands, which had previously been proclaimed to be at the disposal of the nation, issued short time obligations to be redeemed with the proceeds of the sale. In December, 1789, the national assembly authorized an issue of 400 million livres of five per cent treasury bills called assignats. Printed in very large denominations, they were intended for discount with the Caisse d'Escompte, which had the monopoly of legal tender note issue. The assignats were to have no circulatory power, except that they were to be accepted from purchasers of national land. When received in this way they were to be destroyed, but no provision was made for the automatic withdrawal of assignats when the land was paid for by other means. In April, 1790, when interest on them was reduced to three per cent they were declared Iega] tender, without, however, the obligation to receive them at par with other types of lawful money.
Loan of S750,000,000

All we need to do is to ponder that passage to see that at the beginning the assignats had scarcely a ghost of a chance of succeeding. Practically every card that could be stacked against them was so stacked. Let us review the facts which were brought out. In the first place, the new government could not raise taxes. Then, again, there was a large public debt. There was a growing deficit, which means that when they commenced to issue assignats, they had no alternative; they had to issue them. Naturally after they issued and used the first issue, the same pressure which caused them to make the first issue was on them again.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Could they not sell the property?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: There was no place to sell it; that is where the trouble lay; people did not have the money to buy. We must remember that the French revolution had started, and anyone who knows the conditions of that time must realize in what a precarious state the country and government was. It is strange that Mr. White never refers to that, and significant that the leader of the opposition failed to emphasize it. But if we want to understand the facts, these are things that we must know.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: If it was so impossible to raise money for governmental purposes, why was the majority in favour of the issue so small and the opposition against it so strong?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I think the hon. member will best appreciate the situation by an analogy. If there were to develop in the Liberal party a sufficient number of courageous people who said, "We must find a solution; there is something in social credit; there is some germ of truth in monetary reform"-as the leader of the opposition implied the other day

and that movement grew until there was a majority in the house in favour of it, I fancy that the proposal would carry by a slender majority against undoubtedly bitter opposition. Similar conditions existed in France.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: My hon. friend said that there was no money available in France. How then could the government collect it by taxation?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The hon. member is attempting to question what this book says. If he disbelieves the authority chosen by the editor of this great book, the quarrel is between him and that authority. When this man says that they could not collect taxes, I would say they could not collect taxes.

The assignats were short-term obligations. Again, there was an issue of 400,000,000 livres, five per cent treasury bills. Why did not this man White tell us they were treasury bills? The implication is that they were just ordinary money, which they were not. Let this Canadian government issue treasury bills and try to finance the business of the country on treasury bills alone, finance unemployment relief on treasury bills, and how long would it be before treasury bills would be discredited? They could not succeed. This total first assignat issue amounted to about $80,000,000 in our money, the livre being worth about 20 cents. Now $80,000,000 for that age in France was a colossal sum of money. It was sufficient to tax the productive power of the country almost to the limit to absorb it. Bear in mind that that amount of money was issued in treasury bills.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: How much was issued in the other form?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: They were all treasury bills.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What was the total amount issued in the other form?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I will come to that after a while, step by step, if I have time.
The next point is that they were issued in very large denominations. We have a little evidence as to how many of them were in large denominations in the fact that when the Jacobins took power in 1793 they undertook to withdraw or demonetize all the assignats that were over 100 livres in denomination, and they withdrew 558 million livres; 558 million livres were in denominations over 100.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What was that? Francs?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
One hundred livres I take it. Suppose Canada began to issue a new form of money and each of the new units issued was over twenty dollars, and a man went out on the streets of Ottawa and into the stores of this city to spend that money. Look at the difficulty he would have. Many of the stores would not dare cash that unit. Many business houses have difficulty in cashing a large number of twenty-dollar bills unless the bank is open at the time.
Here is another important point. Every assignat had to foe discounted by the Caisse d'Escompte, the bank which had a monopoly of legal tender note issue. In other words every one of these assignats had to be taken to a bank and changed into legal tender notes because the assignats were not legal tender. Any hon. member can see the handicap under which the assignats were placed. What a marvel it is they did as well as they did!

Loan of $750,000,000
The next point is that the assignats had no circulatory power. The assignats when first issued were never intended to 'be circulated from hand to hand. They could be accepted only for land; they were redeemable only in land. Take any credit instrument whatsoever, any kind of monetary counter ever used on the face of the earth, and let it be issued by the best bank in the world; and with the handicaps under which the assignats were issued it would fail.
There were in addition special handicaps.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Are not our problems
comprised in two compartments, perhaps three? First, whether as a dominion we should issue debt-free money or currency; second, how much of that currency we should issue; third, how we are to get it into the hands of the purchasers. I think these are three pertinent questions.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I think the hon. member was not in the house when I began my remarks. I dealt with that then, and he will be able to read it in Hansard. If he does not mind, I will proceed.
In addition to the handicaps to which Mr. White referred, the assignats were under certain special handicaps. In the first place the government was unstable. Everybody knows that people mistrust the money of a government that is unstable. The government had just established itself in France as a result of a successful revolution, but it was insecure. Again, the whole world was against it, both in sentiment and by war. We can readily understand what that means when we remember the position of Russia. The world was against France in sentiment and against her in war, but before very long a new government in that country had to marshal its forces and fight almost every civilized nation on the earth. Imagine the strain that was put on the assignats! Besides, there was civil war within the country. Then this handicap existed, that people thought the value of money depended on the backing of the money; they thought it was the land which gave the money value. Hon. members will realize that if a given, country had too much money all of solid gold, the gold would depreciate because there would be too much of it. It is not the backing behind money which gives it value; it is the need people have of that money to effect exchange. The people of France did not understand that. As a result they issued money beyond a reasonable limit, as I shall indicate when I come to deal with the amount which was issued. Finally the assignats gravitated into the hands of the poorest people. Let any hon. member imagine himself to be living in Paris back in those
days. We will suppose that he gets $500 worth of assignats, redeemable in land two hundred or a hundred miles away, say as far away as Pembroke, but he cannot leave Paris; what good is that money going to be to him?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Let him go to Pembroke.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
He cannot go to
Pembroke. The result will be that he will not want to take the land, he will hesitate to take the money, and the money will depreciate in value.
I have set out some of the handicaps under which the assignats issue operated. Robert McNair Wilson says at one place that with these assignats fourteen armies were maintained in the field by the French government. With the assignats that new government beat back its foes. The marvel is that it succeeded so astonishingly, and at a time when civil war was raging over a large part of France.
How many assignats were issued? The dates and amounts of the main issues are as follows:
Livres
April, 1790	 400,000,000
September 29,	1790	 800,000,000
June 9, 1791	 600,000,000
December 17,	1791	 300,000,000
April 30, 1792	 300,000,000
July 17, 1792	 300,000,000
Up to December 14, 1792, there were several issues, and issues went on. Between April 11 and May 11, 1793, 1,200,000.000 more were put forth. Month after month, year after year, new issues were made. Towards the end of 1794, 7,000,000,000 livres were in circulation. By the end of May, 1795, 10,000,000.000 were in circulation. By the end of July, 1795, 14,000,000,000 were in circulation. By the beginning of 1796, over 45.000,000,000 had been issued. When you bear in mind that the country had only a limited productive power, you can see without difficulty that there was more money there than the simplest kind of common sense would have caused the government to issue. The chief reason why these people continued to issue assignats was that they had to. They were fighting for their very existence. It was not mainly because there was popular pressure or that the issues got out of hand.
Now, what was the effect of the assignats? Up to the end of the second issue the effect was good. I am going to read from the same book from which the leader of the opposition read, at page 25:
It is true that at first the assignats gave the same impulse to business in the city as in the country, but the apparent improvement had no firm foundation even in the towns.
Loan oj S750,000,000

He does not prove that.
Whenever a great quantity of paper money is suddenly issued we invariably see a rapid increase of trade. The great quantity of the circulating medium sets in motion all the energies of commerce and manufacturers; capital for investment is more easily found than usual and trade perpetually receives fresh nutriment. If this paper represents real credit-
And social credit contends that the credit they issue will represent goods and services, which are real credit.
-founded upon order and legal security from which it can derive a firm and lasting, value, such a movement may be the starting point of a great and widely-extended prosperity, as, for instance, a splendid improvement in English agriculture was undoubtedly owing to the emancipation of the country bankers. If on the contrary, the new paper is of precarious value, as was clearly seen to be the ease with the French assignats as early as February, 1791, it can confer no lasting benefits.
There are other passages in this book and other books to which I could refer, but which I have not the time to read, indicating that up to the point at which about the third issue had been circulated the effect upon the country was entirely beneficial. Manufacturers increased their production to the point at which they had more produce than they could sell. Then the same kind of condition began to exist which exists among us. Unemployment began to result; and that was one of the main reasons why the assignats fell in value. Factories were closed; the assignats were piled up more or less in certain places, and altogether a disastrous result followed. Mr. Speaker, how much time have I?

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The hon. member has
seven minutes.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I believe that what I have said with regard to the assignats is sufficient without further comment to show that when any man undertakes to say the incident of the assignats is an argument against monetary reform, either he is inadequately informed, or he is selfishly using the instance to establish a false impression. There is simply no likeness in any respect between the Dominion of Canada and France when the assignats were issued. If dollar bills were issued by this government where the French issued the equivalent of twenty dollar bills; if those dollar bills were made legal tender where the French assignats were not legal tender, there is no reason why the things which happened at the time of the assignats should happen in this country at all.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me, for I am interested, how he proposes to get these dollar bills into the hands of the purchasers?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Social credit advocates the dividend. There are two main devices which social credit advocates. The first is a modification of the arrangement as to price. Where Canada is now paying twenty cents of tax money from the dominion treasury on every bushel of wheat out there in the west, social credit would pay that twenty cents with government-created money. That certainly would put money into circulation right where it is needed, would it not? That is the first thing. Do I make that quite clear?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Does the hon. member have difficulty in hearing? I want to repeat that statement. The money would be issued exactly as to-day we are being forced to issue it. The other night, when we undertook to use vouchers to distribute the butter, the first step was taken towards the method of procedure which will be universally applied in the new era. The United States are doing exactly the same thing. They will issue purchasing power to the people to enable them to buy surplus goods, and they will issue that purchasing power because the goods are there.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: In other words, the money which is issued for the butter is a straight case of a dole, is it not?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, but the money which is now being allotted and will be spent for the butter could be state-created debt-free money. It could not cause inflation because the butter is there; the very minute the money came to the people's hands the butter would be there to be bought. There would be, there could be, no rise in the price of butter. The money could be issued through two channels. First, it could go into the price of commodities. Wheat in Canada in 1939 is to be given a fixed price. The government has to provide from taxes twenty cents a bushel to give that fixed price. If the government were to pay the twenty cents from newly created money, the mere fact that the wheat was there to back the money would be a guarantee that the money would not cause inflation. A similar thing could be done with other commodities like milk, cream, butter, cheese, eggs, coal and other primary products. This would raise the price of products to the primary producer to a living standard without causing the people in general any taxation; there would be no rise in pricea because the goods were there.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Do you mean the government will buy all the goods?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: No. It will give the producers a subsidy, pretty much as we expect to do in connection with wheat.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Bonus everybody.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: And that is no inflation?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
No. You cannot have inflation unless there is a rise in prices. Does the hon. member admit that? If you have sufficient goods to match the money you have in circulation you will not have a rise in prices and you will not have inflation.
Most of the goods now on the market are being sold at too high a price, and the sales tax accentuates that handicap. There is great need for a reduction in the price of goods. Producers generally and distributors are unable to sell any cheaper than they are selling now. Under a new economic arrangement new created money would be used to pay a part of the price of the goods sold over the retail counter so that the consumer could buy those goods at reduced prices. Surely hon. members can see how that would put money into circulation. That was the question the hon. member wanted to have answered.
Another point is this. The hon. member says that the issuance of vouchers to enable people to buy butter constitutes a dole. You may call it a dole if you wish, but the day will come when we shall recognize the necessity of doing what Professor Douglas of Chicago university advocates on page 279 of the book from which I have already quoted. There will be a social dividend, issued for the express purpose of enabling the people to buy goods and services, to supply the money without which they cannot now obtain goods and services-a lack of money due to their inability to get work.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Suppose people will not sell their goods.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Everybody will go on the dole.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Call it a dole if you will, but the day will come when we shall all recognize the force of Professor Douglas's observations. I believe the Minister of Finance wanted to ask a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The leader of the
opposition the other night put this question: Why has no other country issued money and spent it? Let me tell the hon. gentleman that no other country in modern times has issued money and spent it because-and it is exactly the reason why this government

Of course, it is in French. The assignat was the French way of dealing with credit, and I hope the house will be indulgent while I attempt a translation off the bat. It may not be elegant, but I believe it will 'be accurate.
In accordance with the bankers' theory the constituent assembly ordered the disposal of national property at a value of 400,000,000 francs, the proceeds of which were to be centralized in the caisse de l'extraordinaire, or the emergency bank. By the decrees of December 19 and 21, 1789, there were created 400,000,000 assignats of 1,000 livres. The livre is not a pound, I may explain. This was special currency which was used in France at that time, bearing interest at five per cent. The assignat bond, guaranteed, was supposed to be refunded. The decree of April 17, 1790, reduced the interest to three per cent. The coupons were of 1,000, 300 and 200 livres and then of 50 livres following the decree of October 8, 1790. Then there were coupons of 5 livres, according to the decree of May 8. 1791. At the beginning of 1792, large coupons were exchanged for smaller currency in the denominations of 10 sous, 15 sous, 25 sous and 50 sous. The sou was not the same as a cent; there was a slight difference. From July, 1791, on, the farmers wished to be paid in metal money and not in assignats. Assignats were considered legal and forced currency. They were to be received in public and private banks. " Caisse " means rather a branch bank, but " bank " is quite a good translation. It reminds me of what happened to the " free " money issued by the Alberta government. Civil servants of Alberta were paid part of their salary in that special money; they were bound to accept it and put little stamps on it.

Of course the circulation of money is not confined to currency only. My hon. friends know very well that the number of financial transactions in currency is almost infinitely small. Most of the transactions are in cheques. When there is confidence among the people there is a freer exchange of money; it is the old story of the dollar that goes from pocket to pocket enriching all those who have it. There is one other point I should mention. Money is not an essential. Money may play quite an important part, but money is the accessory rather than the principal. My hon. friends know that. The great mistake of the professors who have taught social credit, who have tried to split hairs, has been that fundamental mistake of considering currency as the principal rather than the accessory. History tells us that since the beginning of time, when stones were used as a medium of exchange, barter has been the principal; and that currency in the form of stones, of camels or of metallic coins has been used simply to adjust the difference in the barter. Let us suppose my hon. friend wishes to buy from me an inkstand and offers in return a penholder. The penholder is worth less than the inkstand; therefore he will have to give me something to compensate for the difference between the value of the two articles. The reason for trade has not been currency. I am willing to sell this inkstand to my hon. friend-of course I speak figuratively, because both the inkstand and the penholder belong to the country and not to me, but I am anxious to make a comparison in order that we may come to an understanding. maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:

It is a strange thing that whenever the subject of money comes up in this house we are always reminded of the terrible effects of inflation, but we never hear one word about deflation-never. A great deal has been said this afternoon about the French assignats. I am not here to deny that they failed and that they caused inflation. But may I quote from a man who should command the respect of every member of this house, Mr. Vincent C. Vickers, late director of the Bank of England, and to-day a director of one of the great insurance companies in London, England. This book was written in 1936.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: What is the title?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The title is Finance in the Melting Pot, by Vincent C. Vickers, late director of the Bank of England. He says:
I have watched for ten years every move, every wriggle, of financial policy. I have seen the effects of the greatest financial blunder the world has ever known-our return to the gold standard after the war-and its effect upon our basic industries, coal, cotton and agriculture.
That is pretty plain language. As I said, it is an extraordinary thing that we never hear anything about deflation. From what have we been suffering these last ten years if not from deflation? I will put this question to hon. members; when has this country or Great Britain ever suffered from inflation? All we ever hear are two examples from other countries. One of them was 150 years ago, from France, when it was in the throes of one of the greatest revolutions the world has ever known, and when the government itself was unstable. The other example is from Germany, which had also been through a revolution, whose government was not very stable, and had had imposed upon it war indemnities in an impossible amount.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We suffered from inflation after 1929.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Pardon me; I would say that we have suffered from deflation ever since.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: As a result of inflation.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I would not call prosperity inflation. It seems extraordinary that if the world is prosperous, if people generally are doing well, then somehow there is a feeling that we ought to be punished for it, that we do not deserve it, and if deflation is imposed on a country we are told that we are paying for our sins-as though prosperity were a sin.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) described the other day, as I recall it, the

Loan of V50,000 flOO
issue of paper money as the same as the effect of taking opium, that it requires ever-increasing doses.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I said that was the result of the excessive issue of paper money, not of an ordinary issue of paper money, because we have that at the present time.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Quite. I do not wish to misquote in the least the hon. gentleman. Although I am not a doctor, and I believe he is, I would say that a better simile would be that inflation is a fever. It is short-lived and sometimes violent, and it leaves the patient in a weakened condition, but I believe it does purify the system in that it burns up a lot of debt. Now, how can we describe deflation? I would liken deflation to a certain social disease which is insidious and is not of short duration. As a consequence of that disease the various members of the body politic decay and rot. We see to-day that large masses of people are decaying. If that disease is not checked it ends in general paralysis of the insane. I 'believe that democratic governments generally are displaying at this very moment every symptom of general paralysis of the insane, because they seem incapable of taking any active steps to cope with tihe disease, and the policies which they are backing and endorsing are policies which are leading up to a general destruction of the whole world, beginning with rearmament.
I have said that every time any new idea in the domain of monetary policy is introduced, immediately the cry of inflation is raised unless the money to be issued is first created by the banks. Often after one of our group has spoken the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) will get up, he will turn around to his followers, and will warn them of the evil effects of what we are advocating. He says in effect, " Do not listen to those people. Their money is no good. They have not the art, the magic; their ideas will not work. Only the banks-"

Now, Mr. Speaker, I

Britain. Let us consider Britain's program of rearmament. They are spending something like S10,000,000,000 a year on rearmament. The money is being distributed to the workers, not in respect of retail goods but in respect of goods which the people will never have an opportunity of buying and which, could they buy them, would be of no use to them.

Quite. I am not saying that he is not earning the money. I merely say that the vast sums of money which are being distributed in Great Britain to-day through

this policy of rearmament are not resulting in a direct increase of retail goods, so therefore the money distributed raises the ratio of money to the amount of retail goods which is being created at the present time. The money itself is being expended on the making of arms and ammunition which do not come on to the retail market. And yet, in spite of that enormous distribution of money, they have no inflation in Great Britain; in fact they still have two million unemployed. As has been said by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, until such time as the unemployed are absorbed into industry there is no possibility of inflation.
I have read Doctor Schacht's statements in a paper which he delivered in Germany. I have read the English translation. In that paper he explains exactly the way in which he financed German rearmament, and it was done purely through the creation of credit, which was used to rearm the country. The wages were distributed among the workers who used them to buy the goods and services they needed. That rearmament policy was financed in that way until the unemployed in Germany were all reabsorbed. Of course, when that point is reached there is no sense in creating and issuing more credit because inflation must then ensue. But until the unemployed are absorbed-I do not say every single man, but taking the problem as a whole-there is no danger of inflation unless it is deliberately brought about. That is possible, and it has happened in the past, and I suppose it could happen in the future. There is, however, no necessity for it. There are more than a million on relief in Canada and there are a good many men who are unemployed although they are not registered.

speechtext:
I say a million, because the number on relief bears a relation to the number of unemployed. Making a rough estimate, I should say there are probably half a million men either unemployed or employed to very poor ends, and I say that if industry were given a chance and properly financed we could reabsorb possibly half a million in useful production. I do not mean public works, because personally I do not believe in large programs of public works. I should like to see industry itself working full blast employing every man who is employable. Our opinion in this corner, an opinion shared by a great many people not only in Canada but [Mr. JaquesJ
throughout the world, and proved in Germany, is that the only way in which this can be done is by adapting finance to the needs of industry.

speechtext: When the hon. member uses the word "money," is he including credit? When he talks about great quantities of money put into circulation in Great Britain on a rearmament program, does he include credit or does he mean specie?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Then why do banks go broke, as they do sometimes?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is simple. It stands to reason that if the banks create more money than there is in existence, which they do; that is to say, if they expand their credit to ten times their cash reserves, which is a common practice, and by law they can expand it to twenty times, that is perfectly all right so long as only 10 per cent of the depositors demand their deposits in cash. Experience has taught the banks generally that they can safely go to that limit of 10 per cent. But if there is a panic, and there was one in Great Britain in 1914 when the war broke out, or in the United States a few years ago, and too many people want their deposits in cash, the banks must fail because there is only 10 cents in cash behind every dollar of credit which is out in the country.

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Why could they not create some more credit out of nothing?

maintopic: LOAN OF S750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
So they could, but the people aTe demanding cash. Ordinarily they are quite content with credit. If I owe a bill and pay that bill with a marked cheque, ordinarily people have no objection; they are extremely glad to get it. But if there is any doubt in the mind of the general public as to whether or not they can get real cash for their cheques
they immediately run to the banks and want to withdraw their deposits in cash. The Bank of England went broke in 1914. I remember that during all the years I lived in England I really believed that behind every five pound note were five pounds in gold. More than once I went to the Bank of England, handed in a five pound note and received in return five sovereigns, and I believed everyone could do that. So I was surprised when in August, 1914, too many people went to the Bank of England to trade their paper for gold, and the bank closed its doors; it was broke. Of course in such a situation no government could see its biggest bank stay broke, so they got their heads together and printed so many hundred million pounds worth of paper notes. Then, when the bank opened its doors, the depositors received those notes instead of the sovereigns; and because the paper money had behind it the authority and credit of the bank and the government, the people accepted paper instead of gold with the result that confidence was restored.
We do not say there is anything wicked about that; in fact, without that provision for the creation of credit, business would be impossible to-day, because there is less than the tenth part of the necessary money available. But there is this danger, that if there is a panic and more than 10 per cent of the deposits are demanded in cash, the banks must close their doors. That cuts both ways. It also follows that if the banks loan more money than there is in existence, the people borrow more money than there is in existence, and when there is a depression, when deflation is decided upon and the banks call in their loans, or, in other words, when the banks make a run on the people, they cannot pay back what they borrowed because they borrowed more money than there is in existence. That is why during a period of deflation the borrowers lose their securities to the banks. They borrowed more money than there was in existence and they cannot pay it back, because the money is not there. And you do not pay in goods; you pay in money.
I hope I have made clear to hon. members that we have no intention of permitting any wild inflation, and so long as there is an unemployment problem there is no danger of inflation up to the time when all the unemployed are absorbed in industry. When that point is reached, any further issue of credit or money undoubtedly would result in inflation.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext:
When this bill was introduced it was my intention to speak to it at considerable length. To-night, however, I shall confine myself to a very few remarks upon the measure.
It seems to me strange that in a country such as Canada a bill of this kind should be introduced at all. It is particularly strange, when we have doctrines from the right and from the left which in some respects are equally obnoxious, that this bill aims only at the suppression of one kind. It seems to me that this indicates an unhealthy state of affairs; it suggests that Canada has not been able wholly to escape the virus of totalitarianism, which clearly shows in this bill. The bill indicates that we have among us people who would suppress the propagation of one set of social ideas while they would allow to flourish unimpeded another and equally objectionable creed.
The purpose of the bill is to prohibit the distribution of communistic literature through the mails. I am absolutely opposed to the purpose of the bill, not because I favour communism, for I do not. I have been in public life more or less for the past twenty years and have been speaking on public platforms almost continually during that- time, and on only two occasions has there been an attempt made to prevent me from speaking, and in both instances the attempt was made by the communist party or communist sympathizers. But after all, that is no reason why I should favour the suppression of the communist party. When I advocate the suppression of ideas which I do not like I come down to the level of those groups who wish to suppress ideas with which they do not agree. I was interested in hearing the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) when he spoke on this bill say that he was opposed to the communist party because they advocated revolution. It seems to me that a country which has not a revolution to look back upon has not very much to look back to.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext: Particularly the country of the leader of the opposition!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext: It was the revolution I was afraid of looking forward to, not the one that I was looking back to.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext:
I quite agree. Every
country which has had a successful revolution is proud of it. I am reminded of an organization which they have in the United States. They had a great revolution there at one time, somewhere around 1776; there is in the United States an organization which calls itself the Daughters of the American
Revolution, and the whole purpose of that organization seems to be to prevent any further revolution from ever taking place in that country. My opinion-it may be wrong -is that there is more reason for revolution in the United States to-day than there was in 1776-

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext: Maybe they regret the last one.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext:
-because there is more injustice there to-day than there was in 1776. That does not mean that I advocate that they should have a revolution. That is for them to decide.
The objectionable thing about restrictions of this kind is that you begin by restricting a certain set of ideas and you end up by prohibiting the circulation of all ideas. I do not know just where the communists stand at the present time, but a few years ago they were extremely intolerant of views other than their own. The danger of suppressing ideas which we do not like was very well put in an editorial in the New York Times, on June 7, 1938. It said:
Conservatives and radicals are both shortsighted when they encourage or tolerate the suppression of the opinions that they do not like to hear. In no country in which freedom of speech has disappeared in recent years has it been wiped out with one stroke. Suppression either has moved from Right to Left or from Left to Right. That is it has either begun, as in Russia, in suppressing conservative opinion and moved on until it suppressed every opinion but that of the ruling clique; or it has begun, as in Germany, in suppressing "Communist opinion and has moved on to suppressing liberal and finally even conservative opinion. Freedom is not protected unless it is protected on all fronts.
Another reason for caution in suppressing opinions was fairly well put a short time ago in this chamber by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when he remarked that it was very difficult to draw the line as to when you should limit freedom of speech and when you should limit freedom of action. I believe those were his words; at least it was the import of them. The truth of that must be very clear. Of course a time may come when that line will have to be drawn, and I think in that connection I might refer to a case which occurred not long ago in Great Britain. In the fall of 1936 the fascists under Sir Oswald Mosley began to make themselves obnoxious by holding street parades in uniform. The British government came to the conclusion that such parades were a menace to the peace of the community, and it decided that parades in uniform would not be allowed, but the government did not suppress freedom of speech for the fascists or the members of

We have in this country at the present time propaganda which seems to me more pernicious than anything which has 'been circulated so far by the communist party, but this bill makes no attempt or no suggestion that such propaganda is to be suppressed. maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT

speechtext:
I will confess to my right hon. friend that I had in my hand one evening something which I was going to use against him, but when I saw this, I decided not to do so. The reference to him which is made here is one which certainly should not be made in the public press about any individual.
If you discover that the confectionery industry in Canada is in the hands of Jews-you are an agent of Hitler.
If you complain because the monopoly of amusements, theatres and corrupting movies is 100 per cent Jewish in Canada-you are an agent of Hitler.
If you wish to work to give back to Canadians the monopolv of their forests, their mines, their food industry, their furniture manufacture, their meat industry, their grocery business- you are an agent of Hitler.
, If yon find that the Jews usurp a disproportionate part of the liberal professions in this country-you are an agent of Hitler.
The whole trend of this article is to attempt to make people believe that the Jews in Canada have a monopoly of the wealth of the country, although, as a matter of fact, [Mr. Maclnnis.l
nothing could be further from the truth. Anyone who will read the lists of the directors of our banks, our great industrial institutions, our mining companies, can easily ascertain who the directors are, and very few of them are Jews. I do not know whether it is worth while reading any more from this publication, but I would point out that while the bill would prohibit, say, the circulation in the province of Quebec of The Clarion, in which, so far as I can see, there is nothing objectionable to anybody, it would allow the free circulation of the sort of thing I have mentioned. In my opinion, it is deplorable that we should have to discuss a measure of this kind in the Canadian parliament.
For many years I have found great pleasure and sometimes have derived instruction from some of the writings of Lord Macaulay, and I should like to read briefly from his Essay on Milton. The paragraphs on liberty constitute, in my opinion, one of the finest passages in English literature. Lord Macaulay here is discussing Milton's share in the civil war in England in 1648 and 1649, when King Charles was beheaded-and not many Englishmen are ashamed of that revolution or of its results. He says:
If it were possible that a people brought up under an intolerant and arbitrary system could subvert that system without acts of cruelty and folly, half the objections to despotic power would be removed. We should, in that case, be compelled to acknowledge that it at least produces no pernicious effects on the intellectual and moral character of a nation. We deplore the outrages which accompany revolutions. But the more violent the outrages, the more assured we feel that a revolution was necessary. The violence of those outrages will always be proportioned to the ferocity and ignorance of the people; and the ferocity and ignorance of the people will be proportioned to the oppression and degradation under which they have been accustomed to live. Thus it was in our civil war. The heads of the church and state reaped only that which they had sown. The government had prohibited free discussion; it had done its best to keep the people unacquainted with their duties and their rights. The retribution was just and natural. If our rulers suffered from popular ignorance, it was because they had themselves taken away the key of knowledge. If they were assailed with blind fury, it was because they had exacted an equally blind submission.
I do not think any words could more accurately describe what happened in Russia in 1917 than these words, penned in 1825. The leader of the opposition referred to the suppression of the church in Russia, but the church in Russia associated itself with and became part of the power in Russia which was suppressing the people and keeping them in poverty and ignorance.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext:
What church?

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext:
I believe it was called the Greek Orthodox church. Macaulay goes on, referring to freedom and its effects:
A newly liberated people may be compared to a northern army encamped on the Rhine i?r the Xeres. It is said that, when soldiers in such a situation first find themselves able to indulge without restraint in such a rare and expensive luxury nothing is to be seen but intoxication. Soon, however, plenty teaches discretion; and, after wine has been for a few months their daily fare, they become more temperate than they had ever been in their own country. In the same manner, the final and permanent fruits of liberty are wisdom, moderation, and mercy. Its immediate effects are often atrocious crimes, conflicting errors, scepticism on points the most clear, dogmatism on points the most mysterious. It is just at this crisis that its enemies love to exhibit it. They pull down the scaffolding from the half-finished edifice; they point to the flying dust, the falling bricks, the comfortless rooms, the frightful irregularity of the whole appearance; and then ask in scorn where the promised splendour and comfort is to be found.
We have heard a great deal of that in the last few years.
If such miserable sophisms were to prevail there would never be a good house or a good government in the world.	.
Ariosto tells a pretty story of a fairy, who, by some mysterious law of her nature, was condemned to appear at certain seasons in the form of a foul and poisonous snake. Those who injured her during the period of her disguise were for ever excluded from participation in the blessings which she bestowed. But to those who, in spite of her loathsome aspect, pitied and protected her, she afterwards revealed herself in the beautiful and celestial form which was natural to her, accompanied their steps, granted all their wishes, filled their houses with wealth, made them happy in love and victorious in war. Such a spirit is Liberty. At times she takes the form of a hateful reptile. She grovels, she hisses, she stings. But woe to those who in disgust shall venture to crush her! And happy are those who, having dared to receive her in her degraded and frightful shape, shall at length be rewarded by her in the time of her beauty and her glory!
There is a great deal more in the same strain. I suggest that some of our people who are fearful of the excesses that may sometimes attend the extension of liberty should read this essay of Macaulay. If they do they will realize that as people become accustomed to their liberties they take them in moderation as they take other things to which they are used, and if there at first be excesses, out of these excesses there will emerge an orderly society.
If we in Canada are going to avoid what has happened in many other countries; if we are not only to keep our democratic institutions but to extend them, make them more real and complete where to-day [DOT] they are lacking, we cannot do it by passing legislation of this kind. We can do it only by 71492-279
granting more and more freedom, extending education, extending the privileges of the under-privileged, giving our people the right to take part not only in the work of production itself but in the operation of industry, bringing them into full citizenship; and then we need have no fear of subversive elements whether from the right or from the left. A contented people cannot be driven to revolution or to acts of violence under any circumstances whatsoever. Uprisings and acts of violence take place only when people are fearful, insecure and suppressed; when they feel they have nothing to lose.
I ask this house to turn down this bill so emphatically that any hon. member would hesitate before introducing such a bill in this parliament again.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OF COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext:
In rising to discuss this bill briefly to-night, I am interested in the avowed objects thereof. The bill is to amend a paragraph in the present act, and for greater clarity of understanding I shall read the paragraph; there is only one. The subsection to be amended gives the Postmaster General power to do certain things, to make regulations to keep the mails free from certain substances which should not be carried, to restrict within reasonable limits the weight and dimensions of mailable matter and to prohibit and prevent the sending of explosives and dangerous, contraband or improper articles. This bill proposes to amend that subsection by adding the following words:
and for prohibiting and preventing the sending of any newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, circular, document or writing whatsoever advocating, propagating or tending to propagate communism, and for greater certainty but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing expression "communism," advocating, propagating or tending to propagate the doctrines or axioms of the third communist international, the communist party of Canada, section of the communist international, or of any group or organization having similar aims and professed purposes.
One of the weaknesses of this amendment is that it deals with only one type of propaganda or agitation that is obnoxious to the great majority of the people of Canada. There are several other types, several other political organizations, advocating doctrines that are not in accord with the democratic ideas of the great majority of our people. This is not a logical amendment because it touches only one of those creeds or types of political ideology that never had their genesis on this continent or among the people who first came here, who developed this continent and made it what it is to-day; but

1432	COMMONS
Post Office Act-Communistic Literature
were doctrines that were imported from Europe at a later date, that had their origin in the slums, in the serfdoms, in the ill treatment of the people in those European countries by the powers that were in existence. Those doctrines are not of British origin; they are not of French origin; they are not of northern European origin, and they are not in accord with the beliefs of our citizens who came to Canada from other parts of Europe to escape the excesses that brought about in the countries they left in central and eastern Europe the doctrines about which we hear so much and which are so much opposed to the ideas of Canadians at the present time.
I see no reason why only one type of these hateful ideologies should be prevented from using the mails. In addition to communism as we know it at the present time we have the doctrine of nazism, the doctrine of fascism, and many even fair-minded people would say the doctrine of socialism, which they believe to be injurious and harmful. But nothing is said about preventing access to the mails for literature or propaganda advocating these types of political ideas. '
There are two or three points which we should always keep in mind when discussing legislation of this kind. The first is that above everything else and in regard to everybody else we must not allow ourselves to be frightened unduly, to become panicky because of such propaganda. We in this country are suffering from some of the disease germs that are floating round Europe at the present time, due to different causes. Much of the unrest we have in Canada is not deeply rooted; a great deal of it is on the surface. Clever agitators, by every means they can devise, are stirring up discontent with conditions that have no relationship whatever to European conditions which caused the disease from which many people are at present suffering.
The remedy for the troubles that do affect us in this country is not to be found in oppression or in preventing the transfer of thought either over the air by public speech or by literature through the mails. All that such legislation can do is to force these ideas underground, and when they are forced underground they become exceedingly dangerous.
I do not believe that any force, either physical or legal, can counteract ideas. If the ideas are wrong they must be counteracted by right ideas, and if they are wise in whole or in part they should be given an opportunity to circulate so that everyone may have a chance to judge them and perhaps adopt them with

or without modification. But to prevent ideas from circulating freely, to drive them underground, does no good whatsoever.
We have seen examples of this in Canada. There is a gentleman in public life to-day who a few years ago was resting in one of our penitentiaries for having expressed his opinions in a public place in one of the provinces of the dominion. To-day, instead of being an insignificant person of whom few people had heard until he was arrested and condemned to serve a term in the penitentiary, he is a hero to large numbers of people. I do not think he has yet attained to public office; but it would not have been remarkable if he had, because in several elections he has polled a very large percentage of votes, certainly not all from people who believe in his doctrines, but people voted for him largely out of sympathy for his having drawn on himself the anger of the authorities for expressing his views in a way that perhaps was not prudent. The result of that action was certainly not what was intended; it gave him publicity and notoriety. So one could find in this country hundreds of cases in which, instead of stopping the spread of ideas that it was hoped to stop, they were simply encouraged. I am glad that this government and this parliament are too wise to believe that the spread of ideas can be stopped in that manner.
Take the one country in Europe which has adopted the creed of communism to as great an extent as possible, professes it as its political doctrine, has made of it a religion and has sought for the past twenty years not only to exalt that doctrine among its own people but to get other countries to believe and accept it. What do we find? We find that Russia was the country in Europe that exercised the greatest pressure on its citizens to prevent freedom of thought, freedom of speech, freedom of association and every other-type of freedom. So, because these people were driven underground, because they had no outlet for their opinions, they were driven to associate together and form their plans in the darkness. There were anarchists, nihilists, syndicalists, socialists and all the other " ists " formed by people who were not free to come into the open to talk and plan about what they wanted. I am quite sure that had it not been for that suppression the Russian people would not have acted as they have during the last twenty years. The Russians are among the most democratic people in the world. I do not believe an3' white people are more democratic at heart than the people of Russia, and I am quire

Post Office Act-Communistic Literature
satisfied that they did not enter upon that revolution deliberately desiring to inflict pain, hardship and death on millions of their people. But because they had been kept under; 'because they felt as one man felt who, tapping his forehead, said to me, "I am a dark man and I don't understand very much about what is going on," when their primitive passions were unleashed they went to extremes to which people in democratic countries are not usually inclined to go, thanks to then-long training in controlling their emotions and sentiments in public. That control has been lacking in what are now called the totalitarian countries.
I say the Russian people did not want to go as far as they did. They had one slogan, one battle cry; land and freedom were the two things they wanted. It was to gain these things that millions of people came from Europe to Canada and the United States. Having come here and found what they could not find elsewhere; having acquired land which, in spite of any mistakes they or we may have made, is still in their possession; or if it is lost, being still able to acquire more land; having acquired and retained that freedom they could not secure in their native lands, I believe they do appreciate the benefits of living on this continent. And so long as we maintain those fundamental principles under which they are able to live and move and make a living; so long as they have access to the land with all its resources, I do not believe they are going to be very dangerous.
So, to come back to what I said in the beginning, the worst thing we can do is panic ourselves into a state of fear in regard to these communists and the doctrines they may seek to propagate. That has happened before in the history of the world. For many years prior to the great war the German government taught its people to believe they had to maintain an immense military machine because of the great Russian bear to the east, which was liable to swoop down and destroy them overnight. They talked of that danger so much that they came to believe in it themselves. So, when the war came, as a result of this fear and their own panic, they were compelled to leave large numbers of their best troops on the eastern front. As it happened, this was a good thing for us; otherwise matters might have been very much more serious for the allies. So I say the worst thing we can do in connection with movements of this kind is to become overly fearful of them.
I do not like communism; I do not like to have it preached in a country like Canada, but I do not believe the ground on which
the seed distributed by these communists will fall is sufficiently fertile to produce anything that might become a menace in Canada. It may be that there are spots here and there throughout our dominion where conditions are more favourable for this sort of thing than they should be, but the remedy is to neutralize and sterilize the soil in which these seeds might be planted. I believe it is a bad thing for our country to have such a large percentage of our people gathered in four large cities. Canada is more than three thousand miles in width, much of it very rich soil, much of it containing great resources which, however, are not capable of easy development. We have a population of about eleven million people, of whom twenty-five per cent are located in four large cities, where even in prosperous times many are barely able to make a living. As soon as times cease to be prosperous they are unable to do anything for themselves and have to be assisted by the municipality, the province or the federal government. To stop the spread of communism, fascism and all these other subversive doctrines, I believe we should adopt policies which would induce these people to go back into the open; to get out into the sunshine, the rain and the fresh, clean wind; to get their feet on the soil, where they would be so much more immune to propaganda of this kind. If we could move fifty per cent of the people from our large cities to smaller cities and towns and into the open country we would not hear so much of these things of which we are sometimes afraid.
I believe this bill, if enacted, would be bad legislation. In the first place it would be ineffective. Anyone clever enough to devise a brand of propaganda that will upset the democracy we have enjoyed for so long in this country and in the land of our forefathers will be clever enough to get that propaganda through the mails without a great deal of difficulty. And if it is made more difficult to pass material of this kind through the mails there will be an added premium on that portion of it which does succeed in evading the censor and reaching those to whom it is addressed. I believe that such legislation would be ineffective, that it would be costly, that it would delay the mails and that it would cause legitimate users of the mails to curtail using them in greater or les3 degree. If such legislation should pass I can imagine in years to come critics on the opposition side addressing the Postmaster General of the day. Of course I am not referring to this parliament or to any of the parties represented here. I can imagine the

But the effective way is not, I believe, to be found in this bill. Nor do I believe the effective way is to be found in some of the measures which have been resorted to in other parts of this country. I believe the effective way of destroying error of this type is to allow it to compete freely in the open market, as it does in other countries, as indeed it does in our own country, generally speaking. The result of that free competition will be the death blow of communism or of any other evil.
I understand perfectly the motive that actuates the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. Lacroix) in introducing this bill. He believes as I do, and as the Minister of Justice, does, that communism is a great danger. The hon. member believes that communism, if accepted in Canada, would destroy some of the dearest traditions and convictions of most of our people, and I believe he is sincere when he tries by this method to prevent its spread. I say to him, however, that finite men are not always Ale to judge as to the best methods of arresting error of this sort. But history should be our guide. Every time an attempt has been made by the use of force, by the denial of freedom, to restrict this sort of thing, that purpose has *always been defeated. Century after century ds replete with instance after instance that every time force and the iron heel were used, no matter how powerful, actually or potentially, the so-called doctrine of error survived iny attempt at oppression.
We shall not stop communism by using a department of government, a department that is intended as a means of transporting the written word of one individual to another, to stop its course. The moment the principle of that department is thus interfered with, its effectiveness as a department is destroyed and no real effort at curbing the error will result. The function of the post office is clearly one of transporting the mails. If I thought this was the effective way to curb communism I would be all for this bill. But it will not and cannot be an effective way. Rather it will lend itself to all sorts of abuses, abuses which, if weighed along with the advantages, will clearly indicate to the hon. gentleman and to others the reason why we should be prepared to resort to other measures to stop the spread of communism. But as the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) said, why stop at communism? Why not step along, if you are going to deal with commun-
