maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
This item in the estimates of the Department of Pensions and National Health covering unemployment assistance brings up a returned soldier problem of great importance. The problem is: What is to be done about the Canadian front line man who, although fit and willing to work, cannot find employment and is destitute. That has been the main soldier problem facing this parliament during its whole life, from 1935 to the present time. It was brought to the attention of the government during each of the sessions, in 1936, 1937 and 1938. During the sessions of 1936 and 1937 it was dodged and sidestepped. Last year the minister stated the policy of the government in the words I quoted to-night from page 1040 of Hansard for that year, as follows:
. . . that the one hundred per cent fit man is not the responsibility of the federal government. If he is out of work at the present time it is due to economic causes and not to war causes.
To-night the minister has confirmed that government policy announced last year, which means a denial by this government that any responsibility in connection with these men rests with the dominion. In other words, under the present administration the destitute veteran who served in a theatre of war-and incidentally served Canada, not a province or a municipality-need not look for help to the government of the nation but must look to his
province or his municipality. Despite his war service and his advancing age he must take his chance with all others on the ordinary relief rolls of the provinces and municipalities. This means that this Canadian government will continue to foist the responsibility for these veterans on the provinces and the municipalities.
I am convinced that the policy of the government, which seems to be to wash its hands of the problem, is both unfair and unsound, and that it should be changed at once. One need not look far for support for such a conviction. In the first place the policy of the government, as announced by the minister to-night and last year, is exactly the reverse of the policy recommended by the government's own veterans' assistance commission, known as the Rattray commission, which was appointed in July, 1936, as a result of recommendations of a special parliamentary committee of that year and of the Hyndman committee appointed by the Bennett government in 1935. This Rattray commission was given the duty of investigating unemployment among veterans and of making suggestions for meeting the problem. It did a thorough job. It held public sittings in about twenty centres, going from coast to coast; it set up honorary advisory committees of representative citizens in about the same number of our Canadian cities; it initiated different schemes to give employment, and to-night we have heard of more or less the fag-end of the schemes initiated by that commission. Finally, in December, 1937, eighteen months after its appointment, the Rattray commission brought in a comprehensive report. The principal recommendation contained in that report is at page 63, as follows:
After giving the matter considerable thought and bearing in mind the representation made by organizations throughout the country, by honorary local committees, and information obtained from various sources, the commission has come to the conclusion that it can do no less than recommend that the dominion government accept responsibility for all indigent unemployed veterans who were domiciled in Canada at date of enlistment and who saw service in a theatre of actual war.
This refers to our fighting men; and the key words of this recommendation by the government's own commission are these:
. dominion government accept responsibility." That recommendation is in line with the recommendations of the Hyndman committee which reported in 1935. In order to show the stand that committee took even at that early date I will read from page 5 of the report:
... we are of the opinion that Canada as a whole would shrink from any policy which would permit these unemployed non-pensioners
Supply-Pensions

and National Health
to remain in want and dire distress, as some of them undoubtedly do, and would approve of reasonable assistance being extended to them during temporary unavoidable idleness, until such time as occupations suitable to their ability can be found.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Where is that to be found?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
On page 5 of the report of the Hyndman committee, in the second paragraph from the top of the page. It is also in line with the recommendations of the special parliamentary committee of 1936 and with at least the spirit of the Veterans' Assistance Commission Act passed by this very parliament in 1936, being chapter 47 of the statutes of that year. All these bodies recommended or contemplated that the dominion government would accept at least some responsibility for the indigent, unemployed, front line veteran.
There are other reasons for saying that the policy of this government, that of washing its hands of the problem, is unfair and unsound. In the first place these veterans who, remember, must have seen service in a theatre of war, were pre-aged by that service. In his statement last year the minister said that the war had nothing to do with their being unable to get work. One actual fact is, (however, that these men are pre-aged. Dominion governments admitted that, to the extent of ten years, when they provided for an allowance for these men at the age of sixty, instead of at the old age pension qualification age of seventy.
Further, these men are handicapped by their service through loss of training, in the case of the younger men, and through being away from their employment, in the case of the men who were employed before they enlisted and they had difficulty in readjusting themselves when they got back. The men here concerned are the men who fought for Canada, but who have been unable to readjust themselves and to get established since coming back.
Another reason why I say the policy is unfair is that the average age of these unemployed veterans is about fifty years, and it is almost impossible to-day for any person, whether he be a soldier or a civilian, to get work at that age. Another reason is that these men served Canada-not a province or a municipality, as I said before. While this fact is not recognized by the dominion, it is very clearly recognized by the provinces and municipalities, and also by the veterans. I would refer the committee again to the report of the Rattray commission. This time I turn [Mr. Green.)
to page 19 where the situation is summed up in a few words, as follows:
. To the veteran, relief is something which is given reluctantly-
And I stress that word, because it is absolutely true, and expresses the situation.
-by a governmental body-usually his municipality which he does not consider the governmental authority that really should look after him.
Another reason is that the number of veterans affected by the recommendation is under 10,000. According to the minister tonight, the numbers are dropping all the time. At present there may be several thousand less than 10,000, so that there are not many men involved, and under its ordinary relief payments to the provinces the dominion government is already paying a substantial portion of the relief for these men.
Finally, I say the government's attitude is unfair and unsound, on moral grounds. I think the picture may best be presented by quoting from a letter I received a few days ago from a veteran who served in the first Canadian division, one of those men who belonged to the old red patch division. He said this:
I would be very glad if you could give assistance in a matter affecting veterans of original first Canadian division now on relief rolls through Canada.
Think of the disgrace of that-that we should have men of the old division on the relief rolls of Canada.
In order to commemorate in a fitting manner the twenty-fifth anniversary of our formation for overseas service, and also the visit of their majesties, your aid as an M.P. and a veteran is asked, to have such veterans of original first division removed from relief rolls by having the benefits of war veterans' allowance extended to them.
One cannot, of course, ask for preferential treatment for the men of one division over those of another. I point out, however, that this letter sets out the moral obligation of the Dominion of Canada. On Sunday morning, at the unveiling of the national war memorial, I was struck with the thought that probably there were war veterans in the group on parade who were unemployed, could not get work, and were on relief rolls. Those men would have to go back from the parade, where so much fuss was made over them, to a life in which there is no hope for themselves and in which there is not a fair opportunity for their children.
The government having denied responsibility for these veterans, there is not much point in suggesting methods of aid. In any event the

Supply-Pensions and National Health
methods are for the government to decide, once they get over the hurdle of accepting responsibility. I suggest, however, there are several methods by which aid could be given to these veterans, and I would ask the minister to set out the attitude of the government towards the methods I shall enumerate.
First of all, there was the recommendation of the Rattray commission that these men be paid by the Department of Pensions and National Health-they asked that because the men are soldiers they be paid by that department-a provisional economic allowance for such time as they may be unemployed. That was one method. Another method would be to make provision for these veterans by an extension of the war veterans' allowance, and to show the committee the attitude-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Did the hon. member say the Rattray commission recommended that we should extend the war veterans' allowance?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No. I said that was a second possible method of assisting these men. I had dealt first with the recommendation of the Rattray commission, and I have now gone on to a second suggested method.
In the report of the department for the fiscal year 1937-38, at page 85, we find a statement by the chairman of the war veterans' allowance board, for whom everyone who has had any dealings with the board has a kind word to say. I think his opinion is worthy of consideration, and this is what he said:
Receiving assistance in the form of war veterans' allowance has removed anxiety with respect to the future, from the minds of a great number of ex-service men, and will undoubtedly result in prolonging their days. They display a decided preference for this form of assistance granted in recognition of their service, than for any other form of social security.
A third possible method of aiding these unemployed, fighting men of Canada would be that of greatly extending the government's activities to rehabilitate these veterans. The government made a start in this direction, but it soon grew weary. After listening to explanations given to-night as to just how far this scheme has gone and that scheme has gone, it is absolutely clear that no new jobs, or very few such jobs, can be expected by these men, if the department continues along in its present course. Last year the minister admitted that no, or very little, further provision was being made for new jobs.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Well, I will just read what the minister said as it appears at page 3281 of Hansard for 1938:
Mr. Green: These schemes are all very much worth while, but does not the minister think that during this coming year it is likely that
very few additional men will be helped by the .projects; that it will be largely a matter of continuing help to men already working under them?
Mr. Power: It is quite possible.
Mr. Green:	For that reason it seems important that every effort should be made to work up some new projects.
Mr. Power: I must have a project in order to spend money on it. We have explored pretty thoroughly every project submitted. I cannot just spend money for the sake of spending it.
Mr. Green:	The result, I suppose, will be
that a great many unemployed veterans will not be placed in any work or covered by any government provision.
Mr. Power: It is quite possible.
To-night the minister said we have only one project in contemplation across the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That does not mean to say they will not get employment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The vote this year for pro-bational training is $50,000 less than last year's vote, and the vote for new projects is $85,000, the same as last year. That is a very small gun to shoot this big bird of veteran unemployment. There is little chance of additional jobs, and it is obvious to all that the present projects and schemes cannot do the trick. Doubtless there are other methods of aid, but the government makes no proposal whatsoever, and actually denies any responsibility for these men.
In conclusion, may I say this? As a returned man it is all rather discouraging and hard to understand, especially when one remembers the pride Canada took in these same fighting men not very many years ago, and when one remembers the services which these veterans and their more fortunate comrades have rendered since the war in holding Canada steady and in being prepared to make further sacrifices for their country should the need arise. That was shown clearly by their attitude during the crisis of last September, and more recently by their action within the last few weeks in registering for service under the veterans' survey.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I wish to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) upon his vigorous plea on behalf of the unemployed veterans, and I associate myself heartily with his words. For three years we have urged that definite steps be taken by the government to assume a larger measure of responsibility with respect to the unemployment needs of the Canadian veterans who are destitute. Our plea for the ex-service men in these three sessions has been based on the reports of two commissions which investigated the problem thoroughly, and
4444	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
which were appointed by two different administrations. The reports of these commissions revealed the pressing and tragic nature of the problem. Of that there can be no dispute. Both these commissions made admirable attempts, in my opinion, to formulate constructive proposals which might meet the situation.
Coupled with the representations of these two commissions has been the cooperative endeavour of the organizations of ex-service men, which patiently and quietly have placed evidence before the government in recent years with respect to aspects of the unemployment problem which have caused them grave concern. It must be said to their credit that their representations have been reasonable as well as convincing. It is an open secret that conference after conference has been held to pave the way towards a satisfactory solution of this vexatious question. Until recent weeks there was a general expectation that the government would make some attempt to ameliorate the existing distress amongst unemployed veterans. The minister has introduced other measures which have proved of great benefit, and for these I desire to give him full credit. But in addition there has been an almost pathetic confidence that in this particular he would round out the departmental program and deal with the most vital problem confronting veterans to-day.
The minister's statement to-night rejecting any acceptance of responsibility in this matter, and as communicated to the veterans only a few weeks ago, has caused general dismay and even alarm. I have had abundant evidence in letters and telegrams I have received in recent weeks that there has been indeed more than dismay and alarm. In these letters and telegrams there has been a note of indignant protest that no action has been taken by the government to implement the main recommendations of the veterans' assistance commission as well as of the Hyndman committee. In this respect the government has brushed aside, as it were, the earnest and reasoned plea advanced on behalf of the men in urgent need. From my knowledge of conditions in Canada to-day I am bound to join in this protest. I am convinced that if the government so desired it could have taken steps in the direction indicated by the veterans' assistance commission which would have relieved the situation without placing too great a burden on the national treasury.
I submit that the situation presents a problem which can be dealt with only by the federal government.

It has been reliably estimated from reports which have reached me that there are over twelve thousand veterans with meritorious service to their credit who are at present unemployed and on relief, including those in both urban and rural districts. We know, as a result of an estimate based on a special registration that the Rattray commission found that at least ten thousand veterans were in this category. This is in addition to the five thousand which were provided for by last year's amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
I would point out that the unemployment problems of the veterans have been greatly aggravated in consequence of the services which they rendered to the country. They now average fifty years of age and find it increasing!}' difficult to compete in the general labour market. They are not now regarded as eligible for the war veterans' allowance, or pension with unemployment assistance from the federal department. A special effort on the part of the federal government might even now place many of these men in employment for which they are adapted. Direct and temporary aid is an essential requirement in order to carry [DOT] through any general plan of rehabilitation.
Two commissions have advanced cogent reasons why this problem is the special responsibility of the federal government, and as the hon. member for Vancouver South said, their reports were made after evidence had been heard from all parts of Canada, and had been carefully analysed, and all proposals and suggestions carefully appraised.
The enactment of the Veterans' Assistance Commission Act laid the foundation for a national enterprise which, by relating various forms of assistance, might have brought us within striking distance of a final solution of the problem of the veterans. Honorary committees of representative business men were enlisted in the scheme in order that the full cooperation of employing interests might be obtained.	The commission has now been
discharged and its report has been shelved. The whole scheme is being allowed to fall to pieces because of the unwillingness of the federal government to assume responsibilities that properly rest upon it. The unemployed veteran is faced with the bitter realization that the government is not interested, and as a matter of fact never was interested, in his unemployment needs. The issue is not whether this or	that	proposal is satisfactory
to the government. The issue is whether the federal government should accept in whole or in part any further responsibility with

Supply-Pensions and National Health
regard to the unemployed needs of the veterans now rated as fit and therefore not eligible for benefits under existing legislation.
Two commissions have said that in the national interests this responsibility should be assumed by the federal government at least in part on a temporary basis. But on one pretext or another these representations have been flatly rejected because the government will not admit that the federal government has any further responsibility in the matter. The practical result is that thousands of veterans are thereby condemned to a hopeless destitution until they are so broken down that ultimately there is no alternative to making them recipients for the rest of their days of the war veterans' allowance. No steps are being taken now to alleviate their distressing condition, and I urge that action be taken by this federal government before it is too late to seize the opportunity of rehabilitating these men.
I believe, as does the hon. member for Vancouver South, that our veterans, particularly the front line men, are deserving of better treatment. They have recently given a remarkable demonstration of their loyalty and devotion to the national interests. The nationwide response to the veterans' survey, which was welcomed by the government, has revealed their readiness to serve their country again. The spirit and discipline shown by ex-service men not only recently but during the depression have been exemplary and have earned commendation on all sides. Their offer of service was freely tendered, without any suggestion of bargaining. Through all these years all they have asked on their own behalf is the opportunity to make a decent living. There is abundant evidence in almost every community that a large percentage of them are without that opportunity to-day, and will never gain any such opportunity except through action by the federal government.
A distressing situation has existed in all our principal cities in recent months, during which the hostels and billets maintained by charitable organizations were taxed to their utmost capacity to shelter ex-service men. It has been particularly distressing to note that the transient unemployed have included a large number of our ex-service men. It is particularly heart-breaking that during recent ceremonial parades many veterans were reluctant to participate because they felt keenly about their shabby appearance. Certainly it is true, as I found by mixing with them during recent days, that many more than the general public realized are on relief and under a distinct handicap in showing their loyalty at this time. I submit that
the government could make no better investment than by generous action which would maintain the morale of Canada's ex-service men. That morale can easily be destroyed by the evidence that men who have served and are still willing to serve are left in misery and want. Such a situation is a national disgrace. One aspect of it has been stated in admirable language in an appeal published by the Canadian Legion in the Vancouver press. It is headed, "Canadian legion appeals for justice." They felt it necessary to bring their case to the attention of the public, and I think it states the case so well that I am justified in detaining the committee while I read this statement:
Canada has done much for her veterans, but Canada has not yet completely acknowledged the obligation accepted by Sir Robert Borden, war-time premier of the dominion, on behalf of our people, nor has Canada fulfilled the promises made in an address given by Sir Robert to the troops in France in the year 1917. We quote from that memorable speech:
"You are men actually facing the enemy day and night. You are suffering greatly from fatigue, over-strain, and lack of rest. The marvel of it is that men could undergo such a strain without breaking; but you have never yet broken, and history will appreciate that in days to come.
"You men are about to enter one of the most serious engagements that ever faced the Canadian corps. I can not, at this moment, give any information as to where this attack will be staged. Whether it be successful or not, it is to be borne in mind that it will not be an easy success. . . . AVe feel confident that you will succeed where others failed; for you have never yet failed in anything you have set your hand to, as a Canadian corps.
"You can go into this action feeling assured of this, and as the head of the government, I give you this assurance: that you need have no fear that the government and the country will fail to show just appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done.
"The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion, that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire, and that no man, whether he goes back or remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died."
The fact is that there are some thousands of ex-service men who served in a theatre of actual war, some with dependents and some without, who are on the verge of destitution, and have been in that position for a year or two.
For a number of years the Canadian Legion and other veteran organizations have been active in directing the attention of the government to the unfortunate plight of these men.

Supply-Pensions and National Health
In March, 1935, the legion's representations were given attention by the R. B. Bennett government, and the Hyndman committee was appointed to carry out an investigation into existing facilities for the care and maintenance, while unemployed, of ex-service men.
In a report dated May 23rd, 1935, the committee recommended that the dominion government should assist in payment of relief assistance to the unemployed veteran. The recommendation was not accepted by the government.
As unemployment conditions had not improved, the Canadian Legion approached the Mackenzie King government in regard to the problem, and on June 23rd, 1936, the Veterans' Assistance Act was assented to, and a commission of three appointed to investigate the situation.
The veterans' assistance commission spent about eighteen months investigating the existing facilities for the care and maintenance of unemployed veterans, and in the course of its duties travelled Canada from coast to coast.
The commission, in referring to the claim of the veteran to special privileges, said:
"We feel that the veteran has a valid claim to special privileges. Not only is the dominion government under a heavy debt of obligation to the veteran because of his response to Canada's call in her hour of greatest need, but there has been repeated recognition of that obligation. We have already urged that the obligation is not merely sentimental, but contractual. We feel, as we are confident the country at large feels, that no matter what Canada has done to requite the services of her veterans, her obligation to them is not discharged while one of them walks the streets vainly in search of work, or while one of them is in distress. Canada has a general obligation to all her citizens to provide them with work and to keep them from actual want. Canada has a special obligation to her veterans."
The conditions that the commission found amongst unemployed ex-service men and their dependents in Canada, amply corroborated the views as expressed in the Hyndman committee report of May, 1935, and the veterans' assistance commission in its final report dated December 1st, 1937, made the following recommendation concerning employable or supposed to be employable ex-service men:
"That in the case of unemployed indigent veterans who are not in receipt of disability pension and who served in his majesty's forces in a theatre of actual war and were domiciled in Canada at time of enlistment, unemployed assistance in the form of a provisional economic allowance be granted during such time as they are unemployed, through the Department of Pensions and National Health."
The Canadian Legion feels that a man who answered his country's call and saw service should be entitled, as of right, to remunerative employment, and failing such employment, to adequate maintenance, providing he has the will to work.
The legion through its membership has exercised a steadying influence in Canada throughout the years of depression, and we have reason to expect that recommendations of the veterans' assistance commission, as endorsed by the legion, should receive kindly consideration from the Mackenzie King government.
We are not forgetful of the attention given to some of our requests by governments of [Mr. MacNeil.l
Canada, but we have in mind that Canada carried out its promises as contained in victory bonds to investors during the great war, and we therefore believe that it is quite fair and just that we now ask the present government to honour the promises made on the battlefields of Europe by one of Canada's distinguished men-the late Sir Robert Borden.
We believe that the people of this dominion agree with us that there should be no repudiation in this regard.

I agree with the conclusions expressed in this appeal to the general public.
But there are, in my opinion, otiher important reasons why unemployment among veterans has a special claim on the federal government. In the majority of cases of which I have had experience, service was definitely a contributing factor to their present distress. The average veteran lost time while on active service. He lost educational advantages. He was uprooted from his moorings industrially. He probably lost the advantage of technical training. He experienced extraordinary difficulty in securing a foothold in the national enterprises on his return from service. Many of them had not become firmly entrenched in industry when the depression overtook this country, and they were therefore placed at a special disadvantage during the depression. There is now, as pointed out by the Rattray commission, a residual number of somewhere between ten and twelve thousand who are still under that special handicap.
Usually, although these men are described as being fit, there is some degree of incapacity related indefinitely to service. That has been my experience, and that fact is mentioned repeatedly in correspondence which is directed to me. I think that is clear as we analyse the statistics recently made public by the war veterans' allowance board. I understand that when the new amendment was finally made operative they were deluged with applications. From April 1, 1938, to December 31, 1938, some 12,793 applications were received in Ottawa. As of December 31, 1938, the board disposed of 10,000, of wihich 5,550 applications were approved. I understand there are some still outstanding, but I think it must be admitted that while it is not possible to prove that in many of these cases which were rejected the men were incapable of maintaining themselves through economic handicaps combined with physical or mental disability,

Supply-Pensions and National Health
nevertheless they were pre-aged, there was some degree of incapacity, some contributing factor consequent upon service, which has placed them at a special disadvantage in seeking employment. In addition to that, there is the fact that they are now of the average age of fifty years, an age when their absorption into industry is becoming increasingly difficult. As a matter of fact there is no form of economic recovery in this country which would now provide for their absorption into industry on anything like a permanent basis without a special dominion effort. These I think, are important reasons why the federal government should assume some additional responsibility.
In the Rattray report an important point was made, of which no official cognizance has been taken. I think it should be repeated here now. There is no constitutional barrier which prevents the federal government from taking definite action in this respect. The Rattray commission reviewed social legislation generally in Canada and referred to the difficulties arising from a conflict between dominion and provincial jurisdictions. They had this to say:
The typical veteran wants no special privileges. He was glad to serve his country. He asks no reward for services. We think that we express the feelings of the vast majority of our fellow ex-service men when we say that the veteran resents bitterly having to come cap in hand to the government for benefits that should be within the reach of every citizen of the country. In pleading for social legislation the veteran pleads for legislation that will reach all classes.
But unhappily far-reaching social legislation is not within the power of the dominion government. The veterans' assistance commission is hopeful that, as a result of deliberations of the royal commission on the relations between the provinces and the dominion, there will come a formula for amending the constitution in such a way as to make constitutional a program of legislation that will include unemployment insurance, health insurance, and a revision of the old age pension laws. The veteran, however, cannot wait for legislation of that type.
They go on to say that the veterans as a group present no constitutional difficulty with respect to action dealing with unemployment needs. The federal government could, in my opinion, assume this responsibility, and in doing so, would meet with the general approval of the Canadian public and would not precipitate any serious difficulty with regard to dominion-provincial relations. As a matter of fact I cannot see any great obstacle in the way of a program of general rehabilitation. From time to time the minister has raised objections to a number of recommendations of the Rattray commission. He said it might lead to the establishment in Canada of what
would be the equivalent of a general service pension. That was not contemplated in the recommendation, nor can I see that the recommendation leads to that result. They suggest a temporary economic allowance, and they suggest further that such direct aid should be extended in definite relation to various employment schemes to be conducted under the local honorary committees. There is a distinct difference 'between granting a pension or an allowance merely for service and granting direct aid as a scheme auxiliary to a general program of rehabilitation. I consider direct aid from the federal government an essential requirement of any program of rehabilitation that may ibe initiated by the government at this time, and if the two are related in a common sense way, and if the government will stimulate rather than discourage schemes or projects for sheltered employment or for special employment placement of veterans in industry, there will be no danger of creating the establishment of a general service pension.
Again, the minister said that the veterans themselves were not in agreement as to the details of the scheme. I think the negotiations during recent months have shown that all organized veterans are essentially in agreement on the underlying principle, that is, that the federal government should accept responsibility for this problem; and only by the government's acceptance of such responsibility can the problem achieve solution. Certainly that quibble as to disagreement with regard to the details of the scheme should not be seized upon as a pretext for unwillingness to accept the underlying principle.
If the proposal of the Rattray commission is not acceptable to the government, the onus rests with the government to advance a satisfactory alternative. On several occasions the minister has admitted the existence of the problem. He admitted, and I do not think an attempt is made to deny it, that there is acute distress among this particular group of veterans; but he said that he could not accept these recommendations, and as yet he has not advanced any other alternative. True it is that many have benefited by the enactment of the recent amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act, but that still leaves untouched the problem stated by the Rattray commission, which at that time affected 10,000 men with service in a theatre of actual war.
The hon. member for Vancouver South has given all the principal arguments in support of the acceptance of this principle. I will not traverse the same ground, but there is one point which I think should be emphasized. If the government fails to accept responsibility

in this regard, the only remaining alternative will in the end prove quite as costly. The only alternative left for these veterans is to apply for relief in the municipalities in which they reside. That relief is not usually administered in such a way as to bring them into contact with employment opportunities of which they can satisfactorily avail themselves. As a matter of fact, by reason of their age, and of the general attitude of the municipalities, they are at a special disadvantage at this time in securing employment. Many of them are employable and are willing to work. Many of them, as has been proved by the work of the honorary committees, can be placed in employment if satisfactory or efficient employment placement methods are followed. But if they are left on relief and are allowed to drift along, suffering the deterioration that inevitably follows life on relief; if they are compelled longer to endure these distressing handicaps, they will break down and lose the opportunity for rehabilitation.
My whole argument is based on the idea that if action is taken now, many more men may secure permanent employment and make some provision for their old age or for the future of their families. But if they are left to drift under present circumstances on relief in the municipalities they will ultimately break down and will ultimately have to be taken care of under the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. That is why I urge that action at this time would be less costly and less wasteful than to leave the problem untouched.
In this connection I wish to put in a word or two on behalf of the imperial ex-service men. Since last discussing this matter in the house, I have had an opportunity of visiting the homes of many of these men in the constituency I represent. I have gained a more intimate knowledge of their circumstances, and I feel more keenly than ever that while the government may not be prepared to assume direct responsibility for their condition, certainly their condition is so tragic that more than ever is it imperative that the government should negotiate with the British authorities on their behalf. They came here hoping to find a land of opportunity. For a while many of them made a most commendable effort to secure a footing in Canada, but now they are disowned by everyone; and among the transients in Canada, those who are trekking back and forth from point to point, unable to obtain any recognition for work or relief, are included many of these imperial ex-service men. I am not suggesting that those without domicile prior
[Mr. MacNeil.3
to enlistment should be cared for as a complete responsibility of the dominion government, but there is nevertheless some responsibility on the part of the government, because of the circumstances under which these men came to Canada, to make still more forceful representations to the British government on their behalf with a view to having steps taken to relieve their distress.
These are matters with regard to which we should have a statement from the minister. On a former occasion he said something by way of criticism of veterans' organizations in this regard. I do not think that criticism is well grounded during the present year, because they have not resorted to what may be termed pressure group tactics in regard to this matter; they have relied almost wholly on the careful, well-reasoned presentation of the facts within their knowledge to the government and the presentation of constructive proposals, and have placed themselves entirely in the hands of the government. At this stage I think they have reason for disappointment. So far as the organizations are concerned, it should be stressed that their endeavours in this regard are purely altruistic. I have had the privilege of attending a large number of conventions as well as meetings of ex-service men of various organizations, and I find the men in charge of these organizations are themselves generally in fairly comfortable circumstances. They are concerned solely in rendering service to their less fortunate comrades. That is a spirit of service which should be recognized, commended and encouraged. It is in that spirit of service that the government has been urged by these organizations to take action in this respect. I feel it a privilege to support the representations of the organized veterans on this question.

The problem of the returned man who finds himself out of work and unable to obtain work is, we believe, entirely a responsibility of the dominion government, not of the provincial governments or of the municipalities. It is quite true that unemployment among returned men is only a part of the larger problem of unemployment. That is something which is admitted by all. Recommendations have been made to this parliament by a committee set up by this parliament early in its life. We commend it to the minister; we should like to see him pay that allowance to these returned men who find themselves out of work. We believe, and I think the minister will agree with us, that it is entirely a question of money, and the failure of the minister to put into effect this particular recommendation is on account of the fact that his hands are tied. We suggest to him that he take a definite and vigorous stand on this matter. Let the Minister of Pensions state honestly that he cannot carry out this recommendation because the money is not available. Let him tell this committee that he would take care of this matter if the money were available. Then we believe it to be the duty of this parliament to bring pressure to bear upon the Minister of Finance to find the money to bring economic security to these men, who at one time fought so nobly for their country, and to their families.

I will now return to the subject which I was discussing. Our first duty is to those who suffered during the war, and their dependents. I have endeavoured through pension legislation, through the War Veterans' Allowance Act, and through the extension of hospitalization privileges to front line veterans, to look after those people first. That is my duty; that is my job. That is the duty the people of Canada think devolves upon the Minister of Pensions. I am quite sure the very great majority of the people of Canada have no idea of what is meant by economic allowance; that economic allowance, a term which as yet is ill defined, in the minds of those who are asking for it means a pension, a service pension, or whatever you like to call it, an allowance to the fit man. speechtext:
As a matter of fact, out of those 7,717 only about 2,000 went on because of age; the remaining 5,000, the number I figured would come on, did so under the amendments to the act passed at the last session of parliament.
When the War Veterans' Allowance Act was introduced in this house, it was figured that in 1949 the number of returned men coming under it would be 20,000. We are now ten years ahead of the estimates made at that time. That covers all those who might have suffered in any way from their war service. Pre-age was mentioned by my hon. friend; pre-age is covered. Intangible disabilities were mentioned by my hon. friend; intangible disabilities are covered. My hon. friend says some of them have to produce evidence, and they cannot do so. His friend from Vancouver said he had every confidence in the chairman of the board, Mr. Walter Woods. So have I; and I think he has also. I know that Mr. Woods, in his discretion, will interpret this act in the broadest possible manner, so if there were any disabilities present in the man, I do not think he will be disqualified from obtaining the veterans' allowance.
That leaves only the fit man. What is proposed for him by the two commissions of which we speak? It is not that the government take full responsibility. The Hyndman committee proposed that the government supplement the municipal rate to the basic rate of $18.75 paid by the department to pensioners. If the recommendations of the Hyndman commission, about which so much has been said, were put into effect to-day in Saskatchewan, it would mean 75 cents a month to a single man. That man would still be on relief. The hon. member for Vancouver South spoke of the disgrace of being on relief. Would the disgrace be any the less if he received from the federal government 75 cents a month in addition to what he is receiving now? That was the report of the Hyndman committee.
The Rattray commission went at it the other way round; they said the first $18 should be paid by the federal government, and if there was to be anything supplementary it should be paid by the municipality. That does not apply to any great extent in the case of the unmarried man, but in the case of the married man the Rattray commission said the federal government should pay the first $30, while anything required in addition to look after the wife and children should be paid by the municipality. That does not involve taking very much responsibility. The stigma of being on relief, if my hon. friend wishes to call it that, remains. It is true
that the Canadian Legion, at its convention, suggested in a much broader way that the federal government take on responsibility. We were then face to face with this situation, that in many instances the non-disabled, nonpensioner, absolutely fit and capable man would be receiving from the Dominion of Canada, provided he had enough children, far more money than a man who had lost a leg or an arm in battle. I still refer to what I said; I do not wish any man who served at Vimy to have just cause to blame me for what has been done when he returned from overseas. I suggest to my hon. friends that if we were to give to the uninjured persons better treatment than we give to those who were actually injured in the service of their country they would have a perfect right to say that they have just cause to blame the government of Canada for the manner in which they were treated.
This is a matter I dislike to mention- but I have to do it, because daily, through telegrams and through agitation which is going on throughout Canada, it is brought to my attention. Daily I am receiving telegrams and threats that votes will soon count, and that if matters are not adjusted along these lines in the way in which those who send the telegrams and pass the resolutions think best, we will suffer for it. Those who like to take advantage of that situation may do so, if they desire. But so far as I am concerned, there is a clear and definite plan of action in the department, so long as I remain the minister of it, and that is to treat the injured and their dependents first, to endeavour to look after war veterans who are suffering from some disability; to hospitalize those who require treatment, and to endeavour to find work at various occupations for those who are unemployed. We have succeeded to the extent that the ratio of the unemployed among ex-service men is far lower than it is among the rest of the people in Canada.
Those are my jobs, and I propose to do them. Whatever may be the political pressure in a so-called election year, I propose to do them just the same. I have repeated that to legion conventions and to soldier gatherings; I have said that this program will not be modified, it will not be altered and it will not be accelerated by political pressure, from whatever source it may come, either within or without this House of Commons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Has the minister taken into consideration the possibility of recognizing Buerger's disease as being traceable to war experience? I think up to the present time it has not been so recognized, and it seems to me it ought to be.
4452	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have discussed the matter. As a matter of fact I have seen some cases at Christie street hospital, and have discussed the disease with medical men both there and here. I am sorry to say I cannot get an opinion from them to the effect that they believe it to be a war disease. But if it is any consolation to the hon. member I have rather come to the conclusion that they cannot say it is not. So some of us think we may be able to convince them along the lines suggested by the hon. member. I do not think there is a definite medical opinion that it is a disease of what might be called sudden onset. I am under the impression that they are not so sure now that it could not have been the result of slow growth over a period of years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I appreciate the minister's response, and I find myself in hearty accord with him when he says they cannot prove that it is not traceable to war experience. Is he in a position to state what attitude has been taken by other leading countries; for example, what is the position taken in Great Britain and the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I would say that in England Buerger's disease developed now would receive no consideration whatsoever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Not even Buerger's disease developed in a returned soldier?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, none whatsoever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What is being done in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Or Australia?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I cannot say.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have some information, which I have not taken the opportunity of verifying, which would tend to show that the United States do recognize Buerger's disease as one of war origin.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have been waiting all night to ask a simple question. I refer to the case of a man who received war veterans' allowance, and who had a few dollars in the bank. The money in the bank-and much more than that-was required to pay for hospitalization of his own wife. Yet apparently he is being discriminated against. His war veterans' allowance has been stopped because of that small amount of money in the bank.
I wonder if that is the policy which is to be followed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is a matter of statutory law. But it would be reinstated, I imagine, as soon as the money was spent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: But is it within the act to allow that man to pay his legitimate debts?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The statute is there; I would not know, offhand. But he is not allowed to have capital of more than a certain amount, as in the case of old age pensions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What would that amount be? He is not able to work, and is not working.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The amount is $730, I
believe.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: This man has only $300.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am sure, if the hon. member presents his case to Mr. Walter Woods as he has presented it to me, he will win it

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Some mention was made of Mr. Woods a few minutes ago, and I am sure all hon. members have the highest respect for him. But if there is any discrimination against certain veterans I believe it would come through local inspectors who, in certain odd cases, might be trying to make a good showing with the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Mr. Chairman,-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, it will not help to shout "carried." We were told last night we could carry on a general discussion under this item. Under item 237, which covers treatment, there is a new class 18; does that include the imperial veteran who might have been domiciled in Canada before the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Not yet. We may be able to extend it later on, but at this time we have all we can do to handle our own people. Besides, there would be some difficulties in our way on account of the fact that we cannot get at the war service records of those imperials. Those records are in England at the war office. At this time this privilege is being confined to those who served in the Canadian expeditionary force, but I have no doubt that after it gets under way we shall be able to apply it to the imperials.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: With regard to the qualification in connection with having seen meritorious service, who decides what meritorious service may be? Is there any basis upon which the decision is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Who decides whether or not active remedial treatment is needed? Is that decided in Ottawa, or by the medical officers in the different centres?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The medical officers in the different centres.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Apparently treatment must be given in a departmental hospital, or a hospital with which the department has contact, and where there is a salaried medical officer. How many of those hospitals are there in Canada, and where are they located?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There are 600 or 700, but
not so many salaried medical officers. As I said last night, we are endeavouring to extend the system having to do with salaried medical officers so that it will cover even the more remote districts. At the present time we have all we can do to handle the larger cities. Only last week I called on the civil service commission to appoint a medical officer at Yorkton, and we will go right down the line.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Where there is no salaried officer, has the local doctor any power to deal with an urgent case?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, not a non-pensioner.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There has been some
announcement with respect to a new military hospital at Vancouver to replace the Shaugh-nessy hospital. Would the minister give me particulars?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If the hon. member would let me pass an item for the Minister of Public Works I could give the particulars right now. There is a vote of 8200,000 in public works estimates for building a new hospital at Shaughnessy heights in Vancouver.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is that the total cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No; it runs over $600,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The total cost will be over $600,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Where is it to be built?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: On the same site. We have purchased property there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is the old building to be torn down?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Can the minister give the number of applications for pension in 1938-39? In the previous year it was 10,450, as appears from the table at page 68 of last year's report. I should like the corresponding figure for 1938-39.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: From April 1, 1938, to March 31, 1939, the number of applications was 10,109.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister a few moments ago said that he had received some threatening letters. May I humbly ask him if they came from individual veterans or from organizations such as the British Empire Service League, the Canadian corps or the A.rmy and Navy.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have had some from associations but not from such organizations as the Canadian corps, the Army and Navy or the British Empire Service League. I have had what practically amount to threats from certain members of the Canadian Legion. Whether they were acting in their official capacity, I have yet to ascertain, and undoubtedly shall in a short time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Under section 13 of the
War Veterans' Allowance Act as it now stands, a single man cannot get any part of the allowance if he is in hospital. A number of these men have a house or room rented, and the rent for these quarters goes on while they are in hospital. Is it not possible to make provision for payment of at least a small portion of the allowance in such instances?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is something which
could be studied. We might perhaps make some progress along that line, but for the moment I call attention to the fact that the twenty dollars which the veteran receives is maintenance, and when he is being kept in hospital he receives three meals a day and his bed, so he is being maintained. Besides that, he gets the comfort allowance of seven or eight dollars a month.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The unfortunate point is that many of the single men who have to go into hospital have a room containing their clothing and, in some instances, furniture, and if that is going to be the attitude of the government, the veteran will have to move everything from his room into the hospital or else be out of luck.
4454	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It was not until a year ago that he could receive treatment, and if my hon. friend will let me go ahead and see how I can extend the treatment privileges I shall perhaps be able to make arrangements to transport his furniture into the hospital for him. In the meantime I think he is doing fairly well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is provision made under the War Veterans' Allowance Act for the payment of transportation of applicants who have to travel to be medically examined for the allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: We can make such arrangements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Apparently the minister has power under the act to take out of a retroactive pension awarded, all the money that had previously been paid as an allowance. Would the minister look into the question of having that altered so that you take out only the allowance for the period for which the pension was made retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is one of the amendments that will have to be made to the act some day. It is an amendment that, I think, is really needed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Why not make it now?
